records.title: Agent-directed image-to-3D asset sidecar
records.summary: A promotional demonstration and documented hosted API workflow in which a coding agent sends an image or text prompt to Hyper3D Rodin and receives a generated 3D asset. It is promising as an isolated candidate-asset sidecar for Aralia and Entity Studio, but the supplied post does not prove geometry quality, back-side consistency, cost, licensing, deterministic output, or safe production integration.
records.problem: Turn a visual reference into a reviewable 3D asset candidate quickly enough to explore props, creatures, buildings, and scene dressing without making an external generator authoritative for project assets or gameplay state.

sources.title: Hyper3D Rodin API introduction
sources.publishedAt: unavailable: the documentation page exposes no authoritative publication date
sources.licence: proprietary hosted service; API and generated-output terms require separate review
sources.provenance: Official Hyper3D documentation inspected on 2026-09-12. It documents the underlying Rodin HTTP API rather than proving the exact MCP wrapper or the social-post result.
claims: The documentation describes Rodin as an HTTP API for image-to-3D and text-to-3D generation.
Protected requests use bearer authentication and the API uses an asynchronous submit, status, and download lifecycle.
demonstrates: An official callable API surface exists for producing 3D assets from images or text.
The service separates task submission, polling, and artifact download rather than returning a synchronous in-process model.
implementationContains: Hosted generation endpoints, bearer authentication, multipart image upload, JSON status responses, and artifact-download endpoints.

sources.title: Hyper3D Rodin quick start
sources.publishedAt: unavailable: the documentation page exposes no authoritative publication date
sources.licence: proprietary hosted service; account, API, and output terms require separate review
sources.provenance: Official quick-start documentation inspected on 2026-09-12. No API key was created, no image was uploaded, and no paid generation was submitted.
claims: The quick start documents single-image submission to Rodin Gen-2.5, permits up to five images, and returns a task UUID plus subscription key.
The complete workflow documents rate-limit handling, failure states, polling backoff, a 20-minute deadline, and download only after all jobs finish.
demonstrates: The API exposes practical integration details and explicit asynchronous failure handling beyond the promotional post.
Accepted submissions report credit consumption, so generation has a measurable external cost boundary.
implementationContains: cURL and Python request examples, environment-held bearer credentials, multipart image input, status polling, HTTP 429 handling, job failure checks, and result download.

sources.title: Tripo GPT-6 Astra 3D character workflow
sources.publishedAt: unavailable: the article exposes no authoritative publication date
sources.licence: proprietary service workflow; Tripo, reference, motion, generated-output, and Blender MCP terms require separate review
sources.provenance: The official Tripo article linked by the supplied post was inspected on 2026-09-12. Its tutorial text and example prompts were read; Tripo Studio, Blender, the MCP connection, and the demonstration assets were not operated.
claims: The article describes a seven-step workflow from one character reference through separate body, head, and hair generation, Blender assembly, rigging, expressions, material checks, animation, and rendering.
It requires a Tripo Studio account, Blender, access to Astra, and a configured Blender MCP connection.
It instructs users to begin with a read-only scene and object check, keep generated parts separately selectable, inspect front, side, and back views, and refine bounded problem regions.
demonstrates: The article provides concrete staged prompts and review gates for neck joins, hair fit, proportions, armature reuse, weights, materials, facial controls, foot planting, and clothing intersections.
The article separates three demonstration assets and creator examples, so they are not evidence that one uninterrupted run produced every shown result.
implementationContains: A documented human-in-the-loop workflow that generates Body, Head, and Hair separately in Tripo, imports them as named parts, assembles them in Blender, reuses or creates a biped rig, validates deformation, and authors or imports a short animation.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of the supplied Hyper3D MCP demonstration as a distinct candidate-asset generation sidecar, not evidence that Aralia has implemented or accepted the workflow.
facts: The supplied X post presents a short one-image, one-agent, one-scene demonstration using Codex and Hyper3D MCP.
Official Hyper3D documentation exposes Rodin image-to-3D and text-to-3D through a bearer-authenticated asynchronous HTTP API.
The documented path accepts one or more reference images, returns task identifiers, requires status polling, and downloads generated artifacts after completion.
The post does not provide the original image, full prompt, MCP configuration, generated mesh, material files, timing, cost, retry count, model revision, or acceptance criteria.
No Hyper3D package, MCP server, API credential, generated asset, or external dependency was added to Aralia in this assessment.
Aralia's committed baseline is dff21bbc292bc508a686979180373c3bbfa86953, while the shared checkout contained 1009 tracked and untracked entries during this assessment.
inferences: The strongest fit is a disposable candidate-asset sidecar feeding Entity Studio review, not direct writes into game assets or runtime generation.
A multi-view input set is likely a more honest evaluation than the single-image promotional path because unseen surfaces and topology cannot be judged from the supplied view.
The asynchronous API and credit reporting can support bounded receipts, but reproducibility and output quality must be measured independently.
unknowns: Back-side and occluded-surface consistency, topology, UVs, materials, scale, normals, riggability, collision suitability, and LOD behavior are unmeasured.
The exact Hyper3D MCP implementation, permissions, tool schema, source licence, and relationship to the documented Rodin API were not verified.
Current credit price, generation latency, retries, rate limits, retention policy, commercial-use terms, and generated-output rights were not approved for Aralia.
No same-input comparison exists against Aralia's procedural generators, existing asset library, manual modeling, or other candidate 3D generators.
recommendations: Keep this as research evidence and do not install the MCP, create credentials, submit paid work, or import generated assets without a separately approved experiment.
If evaluated, use one synthetic project-owned prop with front, side, and rear references and require the raw GLB plus generation receipt.
Route output through Entity Studio as candidate-only data with source, prompt, model, cost, timing, hash, licence, and rejection evidence.
Reject any workflow that writes directly to accepted assets, gameplay data, the repository, or project saves.

experiment.question: Can Hyper3D produce a technically usable and visually faithful candidate prop from controlled multi-view references faster than the current manual baseline without violating cost, provenance, credential, or project-authority boundaries?
experiment.exactInput: One synthetic Aralia-owned low-complexity prop with front, side, and rear PNG references, declared dimensions and material cues, one fixed prompt, one fixed generation tier, and the same reference set for the current manual or procedural baseline.
pinnedRevisions: Hyper3D Rodin API documentation as inspected 2026-09-12
Exact MCP wrapper source and release or direct API adapter revision to be pinned before execution
Exact input hashes, prompt, tier, browser, validator, OS, GPU, and service-reported model revision to be recorded before execution
experiment.expectedOutput: One isolated candidate GLB, one baseline asset, turntable captures, mesh and material validation, task and credit receipts, input and output hashes, timing, network and filesystem logs, licence receipt, and an explicit accept or reject verdict under .agent/scratch.
experiment.projectBaseline: dff21bbc292bc508a686979180373c3bbfa86953; dirty workspace with 1009 entries inspected 2026-09-12T16:17:38+02:00
measurements: Silhouette error from front, side, and rear, declared-dimension error, mesh component and triangle counts, non-manifold and inverted faces, UV coverage, texture resolution, material count, bounds, transforms, and file size.
Hands-on time, wall-clock time, retries, failed jobs, credits consumed, request count, download size, network destinations, filesystem writes, and cleanup state.
Rendered turntable review under identical camera, lighting, scale, and background against the references and baseline.
experiment.limit: Two hours after account, terms, and experiment approval; one synthetic prop, one generated candidate, one baseline, a predeclared maximum credit spend, no private assets, production credential, repository write, runtime integration, accepted asset, publication, or automatic promotion.
acceptanceCriteria: Licensing, security, and operations owners approve the exact service terms, input, MCP or API surface, scoped credential, retention, and maximum spend before submission.
The candidate passes file-safety, format, transform, bounds, manifold, normal, UV, material, texture, scale, and turntable gates with no hidden-view defect that blocks the intended prop use.
Total hands-on time is at least 30 percent lower than the baseline and actual spend stays within the declared ceiling.
The workflow writes only to the disposable directory, exposes no repository or save authority, and cleanup removes credentials, temporary files, processes, ports, and package changes.
rejectionCriteria: Terms, provenance, credential scope, retention, spend, or input rights are unclear or unapproved.
The candidate has unacceptable unseen surfaces, silhouette, topology, normals, UVs, textures, materials, scale, performance, or visual fidelity.
The workflow requires broad filesystem access, repository writes, production runtime integration, automatic promotion, private input transfer, or undeclared services.
Any request, cost, latency, retry, failure, cleanup, or reproducibility boundary exceeds the declared limit.
experiment.isolationBoundary: Only after separate approval, use a scoped disposable credential and a pinned adapter in one ignored directory; submit only the synthetic reference set, download only the candidate artifact and receipts, and pass them through a read-only project-owned validator before preview.
experiment.cleanup: Stop the adapter, verify any loopback ports closed, revoke the scoped credential, remove temporary inputs, outputs, cache, adapter, logs, and package changes according to approved retention, confirm unchanged production source and accepted assets, and append a dated result only if the experiment was explicitly run.

records.title: Video-to-animated-3D reconstruction
records.summary: A research workflow and hosted creation surface for turning a short single-character video into a textured animated FBX. The published VMR artifact demonstrates one carefully reconstructed 52-pose baseball swing with strong export-fidelity receipts, but it does not yet provide trained weights, a packaged reconstruction pipeline, or evidence of generalization to arbitrary videos.
records.problem: Recover editable 3D character appearance and motion from a short performance video when no source rig, mesh, or motion-capture data exists, while preserving contact detail and temporal coherence well enough for inspection and reuse.

sources.provenance: The exact X post supplied by the user was inspected in the signed-in browser on 2026-09-12. It links the VMR research page, blenDojo creation surface, and DiscoSea Hugging Face repository. Its 12-second video was treated as a demonstration, not a benchmark or generalization proof.

sources.title: Pinned vmr3D research release
sources.licence: Apache-2.0 repository designation; third-party methods, models, reconstructed inputs, source assets, and outputs retain separate terms
sources.provenance: Public ungated Hugging Face repository pinned at a22d1f294dfc5874244c34a869d2cca6aaf14c27. Metadata, model card, paper claims, files, and validation descriptions were inspected without downloading the release, running verification, opening Blender or Unity, or executing reconstruction.
claims: The release describes VMR as recovering coherent motion from reconstructed per-frame mesh sequences by separating coarse interior-volume motion from detailed surface reconstruction and protected local repair.

It reports one 52-pose stylized baseball swing at 30 fps, exported as textured FBX with animated blend shapes, author-confirmed Unity playback, and maximum reimported world-space vertex difference below 4.85e-8 scene units.
The release explicitly says it has no trained VMR neural weights, implemented learning architecture, general video-to-character inference endpoint, or packaged original reconstruction environment.
demonstrates: The repository provides an animated FBX, Blender scene, synchronized comparisons, white paper, release manifest, verification script, and FBX validation record for one sequence.

The demonstrated implementation uses 64 interior-volume controls with four influences per original vertex, explicit grip and bat detail reconstruction, protected opening and closing checkpoints, and post-export geometry validation.

Two non-rigid registration refinements and a 64-bone Dem Bones approximation were compared, but the reported visual preference and measurements remain specific to the single sequence and tested configurations.
implementationContains: One baked 52-pose character animation, textured FBX, Blender workspace, paper media, integrity manifest, verification script, validation receipts, learning roadmap, and proposed data contract.
It does not contain a general automatic video-to-FBX implementation, trained checkpoint, or complete dependency-pinned reconstruction source pipeline.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of VMR and blenDojo as a distinct video-to-animated-3D identity. The evidence proves one inspectable baked sequence and a hosted upload surface, not a general reproducible video reconstruction implementation.
facts: The supplied post promotes video-to-3D animation and links a VMR paper, a hosted creation surface, and a public research-artifact repository.
The pinned VMR release contains one 52-pose stylized baseball swing at 30 fps as a textured FBX with animated blend shapes and a Blender scene.

VMR aligns reconstructed target meshes, recovers coarse motion with 64 interior-volume controls and four influences per original vertex, repairs difficult contact detail, protects endpoint geometry, and validates exported playback.
The author reports Unity playback and a maximum post-reimport vertex difference below 4.85e-8 scene units for the stored poses; this is export fidelity, not source-video reconstruction accuracy.
The release explicitly lacks trained VMR weights, a learning architecture implementation, a general inference endpoint, and the original complete reconstruction environment.
The public blenDojo workspace advertises up to three-second upright-humanoid video input and animated FBX output for 30 credits, but no new generation was run or inspected.
No external source, model, video, FBX, Blender file, dependency, account, credential, or service entered Aralia during this assessment.
inferences: The strongest current value is the separation of coarse motion, local surface repair, protected contact regions, and export verification rather than an immediately adoptable video-to-character model.

A baked blend-shape sequence may preserve source-specific deformation better than skeleton-only retargeting but is likely heavier, less editable, and less reusable across Aralia characters and gameplay states.
The hosted creation surface may implement additional proprietary automation beyond the public research release, but that relationship cannot be inferred from the shared branding alone.
The honest status is worth watching until varied held-out subjects, packaged reconstruction, privacy and rights terms, and reproducible general output are available.
unknowns: The hosted service's model, source pipeline, operator involvement, processing time, failure rate, retention, security, output rights, and relationship to the public VMR artifacts are unknown.
No held-out evaluation covers different characters, clothing, hair, camera motion, occlusion, fast motion, non-humanoids, multiple people, props, or interactions.

Source-video fidelity, temporal jitter, topology consistency, contact correctness, texture stability, blend-shape size, playback cost, editability, and compression behavior were not independently measured.
Aralia compatibility with the FBX skeleton or blend-shape layout, coordinate system, materials, animation mixer, equipment, collision, gameplay timing, saves, and browser performance is unproved.
The 30-credit label does not establish monetary cost or a complete pricing, refund, or account contract.
recommendations: Keep VMR as a separate record linked to IB-0007 motion synthesis and IB-0008 image-to-3D assets; do not collapse video reconstruction into either mechanism.
Do not upload private or project-owned footage, create an account, buy credits, download artifacts, or connect the output to production without a separately approved experiment and terms review.
First inspect only the public release artifact against Aralia's candidate-animation and asset validators; distinguish baked export fidelity from reconstruction accuracy.
Reassess when the authors publish a packaged reconstruction pipeline, trained model or explicit hosted-service technical contract, and multi-subject held-out results.

revisions.changeSummary: Added GPUOcean as supporting evidence rather than creating a duplicate ocean record. Its scrolling-noise approximation, shoreline chain, swash film, two-frame foam model, and world-space surface query strengthen specific IB-0001 boundaries while its absent licence and lack of tests block source reuse.
facts: GPUOcean is a source-complete raw WebGPU and WGSL implementation created in August 2026 with 79 commits at the inspected head.
It approximates an FFT ocean by generating seeded band-passed noise textures on the CPU and blending scrolling copies before layered directional sampling.

It combines a world-anchored offshore surface with an authored coastline, signed-distance terrain, a CPU shallow-water chain, a heightless swash film, wet sand, caustics, and separate persistent offshore and film foam buffers.
Its SurfaceQuery returns height, velocity, column depth, and swash contribution at a world position; it uses three fixed-point inversion passes offshore and exact CPU-chain sampling in the film.
The successful Pages workflow deploys the static source but runs no repository-owned tests or benchmark harness.
The repository exposes no licence declaration, LICENSE file, package manifest, release, or tag.

Aralia's current ocean remains a deterministic absolute-time three-cascade JONSWAP and TMA FFT with GPU compute, CPU reference, 60 focused tests recorded in the plan map, and no game-consumed ship-height query, LOD center caller, or shoreline coupling.
inferences: GPUOcean is best treated as additional evidence for IB-0001 because it addresses the same WebGPU ocean, persistent-foam, environment, and floater-sampling decision rather than a separate product problem.
Its world-space SurfaceQuery is stronger evidence for an Aralia-owned ship and floater sampling seam than its scrolling-noise wave generator is evidence for replacing Aralia's FFT.

Its coast-chain and material-space swash handoff identify a useful future open-ocean-to-shore boundary, but Aralia should derive that boundary from canonical terrain and finite-water systems rather than import the demo coastline.
unknowns: The live demonstration's visual quality, controls, mobile behavior, accessibility, and runtime diagnostics were not independently operated.
No published test harness proves numerical conservation, fixed-point error, foam reset, shoreline stability, or cross-browser reproducibility.
Commit-message M3 timings are not reproducible from a pinned benchmark script and do not establish Aralia performance.
The cost and agreement of an Aralia CPU or GPU surface query across all three cascades have not been measured.
The legal terms for copying, adapting, or redistributing GPUOcean code are unavailable.
recommendations: Keep Aralia's seeded FFT, physical spectrum, CPU reference, absolute-time contract, and existing tests as ocean authority.
Use GPUOcean only as mechanism evidence for a project-owned world-space sample contract, persistent foam, and a future shoreline handoff.
Test the smallest read-only height, slope, velocity, and depth query against Aralia's CPU reference before attempting coast, swash, or persistent foam work.
Do not copy source, WGSL, coastline data, constants, or benchmark claims unless the repository later publishes compatible licensing and the relevant behavior is independently verified.

records.title: Terrain-aware spline road authoring
records.summary: A complete standalone Three.js editor for manually drawing terrain-following dirt-road networks, snapping endpoints and intersections, generating river bridges, clearing vegetation, and laying roadside plots and walls. Its strongest fit is as interaction and validation evidence for an optional Aralia authoring sidecar, not as a replacement for Aralia's deterministic generated street network.
records.problem: Let an author lay out and revise connected rural roads over terrain while keeping junctions, river crossings, vegetation clearance, residences, access lanes, and roadside structures geometrically coherent.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment as a new idea identity because interactive spline authoring is distinct from both IB-0001 and Aralia's existing generated-road mechanism.
facts: The source is a substantial modular implementation with road graph, editor, mesh, junction, bridge, residence, wall, terrain, and vegetation subsystems.
The road editor is manually authored through control points and curvature input, then committed into a mutable road-network snapshot with undo and redo.
The implementation uses Catmull-Rom geometry, spatial indexing, snapping, terrain sampling, and water-aware bridge-span detection.
Aralia already generates one deterministic town street network from wards, gates, regional approaches, and routed traffic using a pure dependency-free graph algorithm.
Aralia already shares ribbon geometry across 2D and 3D consumers, drapes edge vertices to the rendered terrain surface, and retains street roles, tiers, widths, and tests.
Aralia's regional and town road facts feed streaming, pathfinding, tactical provenance, town blocks, gate placement, and bridge recipes; they are not merely editable presentation meshes.
The source's deploy workflow builds and publishes but does not run its declared regression scripts.
inferences: The most reusable contribution is the authoring interaction model—preview, snapping, network editing, validation, and undo—not the source's road-generation authority.
Automatic bridge approaches and vegetation-clearance previews could improve Aralia's diagnostic and authoring tools if driven by canonical WorldForge water and keep-out facts.
Replacing Aralia's generated street graph with mutable Catmull-Rom editor state would weaken cross-tier provenance and deterministic regeneration.
unknowns: The live demonstration's actual interaction quality, performance, accessibility, and narrow-screen behavior were not visually verified.
No benchmark establishes road-network scale, spatial-index cost, mesh rebuild cost, or maximum practical control-point count.
The repository does not expose a versioned migration or save-compatibility policy for road snapshots.
Repository-level MIT licensing does not by itself prove the provenance and redistribution rights of every bundled generated texture and vegetation asset.
The cost of mapping an editor patch back into Aralia's ward, gate, street-role, crossing, and provenance contracts has not been measured.
recommendations: Preserve Aralia's townStreetNetwork and WorldForge artifacts as canonical generated state.
Adapt only a minimal preview-and-snap editor around an Aralia-owned patch format if manual road correction becomes an explicit product requirement.
Use canonical terrain, waterline, bridge, vegetation keep-out, ward, and gate facts for validation rather than importing the sample terrain or assets.
Do not add Three.js 0.185, lil-gui, SeedThree, textures, or source modules to Aralia merely because the record is promising.

records.title: Screen-space microgeometry with hole reconstruction
records.summary: A reverse-engineering article argues that Crimson Desert turns height-map detail into camera-facing microgeometry in a compute pass, then uses parallax occlusion mapping to patch holes where screen-space input is missing. The mechanism is plausible and visually relevant, but the claimed engine analysis and WebGPU viewer are not published, so this is a partial technique to watch and reproduce only from clean public inputs.
records.problem: Add convincing surface relief and silhouette detail to broad environment meshes without authoring dense source geometry or relying on a full virtualized-geometry system.

sources.title: Hacking on Crimson Desert with Grok Build
sources.licence: All rights reserved or unspecified; the article does not grant a code, model, shader, screenshot, or game-asset reuse licence
sources.provenance: The supplied X status is a link-only wrapper for an X Article by Grummz. Its platform identifier resolves to 2026-06-05T15:35:32.711Z. The signed-in article was inspected on 2026-09-01; no downloadable findings report, viewer repository, shader dump, or immutable article revision was exposed.
claims: The author says agents used decompilers, model-extraction tooling, shared findings documents, and an iterative dual-path attack on game data and shader or executable code.

The author concludes that Crimson Desert creates screen-space microgeometry from height and normal data, rasterizes it through compute and atomic operations, and uses parallax occlusion mapping as a hole filler.
The article says its WebGPU viewer used extracted game models to visually cross-check hypotheses against the observed effect.
demonstrates: The article embeds videos showing apparent silhouette relief, a screen-aligned triangle grid, and red-highlighted holes near a screen edge with a reconstructed fill.
The article visibly separates its proposed main displacement mechanism from its proposed POM reconstruction stage.
The article documents an iterative research workflow, but embedded media is evidence of a result presentation rather than proof of the unpublished implementation or engine attribution.

records.title: Auxin-driven emergent plant morphogenesis
records.summary: A source-complete MIT JavaScript xenobotany engine in which one cellular auxin-transport solver drives phyllotaxis, vein formation, leaf margins, petals, fruit, and lifecycle effects across different tissue topologies. Its honest negative results and separation of simulation from rendering make it useful research evidence, but its best Aralia fit is an optional offline morphology sidecar rather than a replacement for the current deterministic, environment-derived, instanced vegetation pipeline.
records.problem: Generate varied, internally related plant structures from local transport rules instead of drawing each organ silhouette, vein network, and arrangement independently.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment as a new idea identity: transport-driven plant morphogenesis is distinct from the existing ocean, road-authoring, and screen-space detail records and from Aralia's current formula-driven vegetation generator.
facts: The repository is a source-complete MIT JavaScript implementation with simulation, rendering, export, tests, scientific notes, tuning notes, pitfalls, journal, and a self-contained browser artifact.
Its core CellField solver stores auxin concentration and polar transport and uses local active and diffusive transport across tissue-neighbor graphs.
The same transport mechanism is applied under different tissue topologies and boundary conditions to meristems, leaves, venation, petals, fruit, and later perturbations.
The repository records imposed priors and negative results, including phyllotactic divergence wandering rather than locking to the golden angle.
The pinned continuous-integration run succeeded, but no release or Aralia-scale performance benchmark was published.

Aralia already has a deterministic environment-to-genome-to-traits-to-skeleton-to-foliage tree pipeline with pipe-model allometry, gravity, wind, aridity, light, unit-frame geometry, triangle budgets, and instanced variants.
Aralia's current vegetation explicitly uses a golden-angle constant for foliage and lateral placement and does not implement a cellular auxin field.
inferences: The repository's most valuable contribution is a mechanism and research discipline for generating correlated organ structure, not a drop-in rendering or world-simulation dependency.
A bounded leaf or understory generator could complement Aralia's cheaper biome-derived trees by producing a small library of unusual deterministic variants offline.
Running cell-level morphogenesis per world tree or per frame would conflict with Aralia's current instancing and streamed-world performance model without strong evidence.
unknowns: The live demonstration was not visually operated during this assessment, and no same-camera comparison with Aralia vegetation exists.
Runtime, memory, convergence, and export cost for a representative mature specimen on Aralia's supported hardware are unmeasured.
The stability of morphology across solver step size, browser, and future code revisions has not been established for Aralia's reproducibility requirements.
Scientific plausibility does not establish game readability, artistic controllability, accessibility, or production value.
Vendored Three.js files, the generated artifact, and package-lock metadata need file-level provenance and maintenance review before any code reuse.
recommendations: Preserve Aralia's grown-tree and instanced vegetation pipeline as production authority.
If explicitly requested, test one independently bounded offline leaf or understory asset and compare it with the current deterministic baseline.
Keep facts such as seed, biome, placement, collision, canopy footprint, and save identity outside the solver; accept only derived visual geometry after normal review.
Do not import repository source, vendored modules, artifacts, packages, or scientific assumptions merely because this record is promising.

records.title: Procedural ability telegraph and VFX workbench
records.summary: A coherent family of Three.js ability-casting sandboxes that combines reusable line and zone aim indicators, live-tunable procedural spell effects, GPU particles, pooling, presets, and animation timing. revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of the supplied repository shelf, narrowed to one coherent ability-targeting and procedural-VFX family rather than one record per repository.
facts: The supplied URL is a public repository shelf, not one implementation, release, paper, or demonstration.
The shelf exposed 27 public repositories during inspection; multiple repositories form related ability-casting, water, vegetation, weather, building, geometry-painting, and third-person families.

The primary ability-casting repository contains implementation source for aim indicators, five abilities, procedural shaders, GPU particles, pooling, post-processing, animation, assets, and a live editor.

The primary repository is MIT-licensed and pins Three.js 0.185.1, lil-gui 0.21.0, and Vite 8.1.5, but exposes no release, tag, repository-owned automated test workflow, or reproducible benchmark harness.
Its line and zone indicators clamp range, expose minimum-range invalidity, cancel with Escape or right-click, and recalculate the cursor ray each frame.
The source documents flat y=0 targeting, pale-floor contrast, transparent sorting, always-cleared distortion, and short-range overlap as limitations.

Aralia already owns canonical spell targeting types, target validation and resolution utilities, AoE calculation, armed-targeting hooks and tests, targeting HUD states, Escape cancellation, renderer parity requirements, and a BattleMap VFX system.
The shared Aralia checkout had 645 tracked and untracked entries during inspection, so the named commit is not the complete local state.
inferences: The family is strongest as evidence for an Aralia-owned visual telegraph and effect-authoring boundary, not as a combat or targeting engine.

Metre-consistent signed-distance indicators, live pause-and-tune controls, JSON presets, and pooled procedural effect pieces could improve iteration and presentation if they consume canonical Aralia geometry.
The additional ability repositories are supporting family evidence rather than distinct records because they vary content and aim shapes without establishing a different core mechanism.
The profile's other coherent families may warrant later records or support existing records, but this intake does not establish enough cross-family comparison to classify them honestly.
unknowns: The demonstrations were not independently operated or compared side by side with Aralia during this assessment.
No reproducible measurement establishes frame time, memory, shader compilation cost, mobile behavior, or accessibility on Aralia's supported targets.
The effect parameters, authored FBX, textures, HDR probe, and reference images need file-level provenance and redistribution review before any reuse.
The flat-ground indicator approach may not match Aralia's terrain, elevation, cover, occlusion, camera, and multi-renderer requirements.
The maintenance cost of a large mutable settings surface and hundreds of controls is unmeasured.
The water, vegetation, weather, building, geometry-painting, and third-person repositories remain unassessed; they are neither accepted nor rejected by this record.
recommendations: Keep Aralia's target resolution, AoE geometry, validity reasons, action economy, and gameplay state as the only combat authority.

Prefer a small typed presentation schema and measured presets over adopting the source's complete mutable editor or asset shelf.
Do not import repositories, packages, source, shaders, assets, presets, or licence obligations merely because this record exists.
Intake another repository family only when a supplied source or explicit research request provides enough evidence to establish a distinct mechanism.

facts: The supplied t.co URL redirects to the public NomaDamas/CozyClay repository.

CozyClay is a source-complete browser editor with scene blocking, hierarchy, transform gizmos, camera and lens tools, rails, cuts, prompt blocks, character posing, IK, capture, export, local project history, and MCP control.
The pinned main head is acba8c34a7c10fb11c04f06d56352f07a7e95760 from 2026-09-01T16:36:19Z; release v1.7.0 was published earlier the same day at tag commit 11360e2ae589f8e3bea75cf2b0652c338feb336b.
The main package requires Node 22.13 or newer and a Chromium browser; its source manifest pins React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, MediaPipe Tasks Vision, Mediabunny, PostHog, and Vite.
Optional new-motion generation requires an SSH-accessible NVIDIA machine and Kimodo; the hosted queue adds Cloudflare Worker, D1, R2, Google OAuth, Turnstile, and a maintainer GPU worker.

The local MCP package adds the MCP SDK, WebSocket, and Zod dependencies and exposes both headless project operations and live editor control, including file-writing tools constrained to a project root.

CozyClay code is AGPL-3.0-or-later, and its own notice says two bundled Mixamo FBX files are outside that grant and are not permitted for raw redistribution in the repository, package, or hosted site.
The official npm package sends anonymous analytics by default with documented opt-out controls; source checkouts and development builds say they do not send analytics.

Aralia already has a large multi-window Design Preview, deterministic scenario surfaces, camera controllers, scripted visual-test captures, ignored capture manifests, project-owned CC0 humanoid clip retargeting, and a narrow page-bound WebMCP tool layer.
The shared Aralia checkout had 648 tracked and untracked entries during inspection, so the committed baseline is not the complete project state.
inferences: The strongest reusable idea is a project-owned shot-plan contract connecting camera intent, reproducible captures, and review evidence, not CozyClay's full editor or generated-motion stack.
A detached previsualization sidecar could complement Design Preview and visual-test rigs without becoming gameplay, scene, animation, or save authority.
CozyClay's film-vocabulary solver and shared editor/MCP scene model are useful architecture evidence for keeping human and agent camera operations aligned.
The repository's rapid revision rate, mixed gating tiers, optional services, AGPL obligations, telemetry, and acknowledged asset problem make direct adoption unsafe now.
unknowns: The interactive studio, hosted motion queue, npm package, and MCP server were not installed or operated during this assessment.
No comparison establishes that CozyClay produces faster or better Aralia review shots than current Design Preview, vistest, and capture tooling.
Camera coordinate, focal-length, rig, animation, scene-object, and project-file compatibility with Aralia are unproved.
Accessibility, keyboard completeness, reduced-motion behavior, narrow-screen usability, GPU cost, memory, and teardown on Aralia target hardware were not independently measured.
Kimodo licensing, weights, setup cost, deterministic behavior across revisions, and fitness for non-human Aralia entities remain unresolved.
The date and exact content of the promised CC0 rig replacement are unavailable.
recommendations: Do not install, clone, import, connect, or deploy CozyClay while the upstream package contains the acknowledged Mixamo redistribution problem.
Keep Aralia scene facts, entity rigs, animation clips, cameras, game saves, review verdicts, and WebMCP authority project-owned.
After the named licensing blocker is resolved, test only an isolated shot-plan adapter using synthetic Aralia-owned geometry and no motion backend, account, analytics, or external asset.

Borrow architectural ideas such as explicit shot vocabulary, transactional history, project-file restriction, live-versus-headless capability errors, and reproducible capture assertions through independently designed Aralia contracts.
Append a reassessment rather than rewriting this conclusion if CozyClay replaces the disputed assets, changes licensing, or Aralia gains a canonical shot-plan boundary.

records.title: Neural keyframe-to-motion generation sidecar
records.summary: A source-complete C++23 and GGML port of NVIDIA MotionBricks that generates 34-joint G1 skeletal motion from sparse constraints, movement, facing, style, and seeded planning commands on CPU or Vulkan. It is promising as a detached candidate-motion generator for Aralia humanoid experiments, but its native runtime, fixed skeleton, large model bundle, and separately licensed weights must remain outside gameplay authority.
records.problem: Produce controllable transition and locomotion candidates between sparse pose constraints without manually authoring every intermediate frame or making a learned model authoritative for gameplay animation.

sources.title: motion-bricks.cpp repository
sources.licence: Apache-2.0 for repository source; NVIDIA Open Model License terms apply separately to original and converted weights and styles
sources.provenance: The exact public repository supplied by the user. GitHub metadata and the repository documentation were inspected without cloning, building, downloading its 0.73 GB model bundle, or executing code.
claims: The repository describes an end-to-end C++23 and GGML implementation of MotionBricks G1 inference with CPU and Vulkan behind one C API.
The README reports strict CPU parity across fourteen captured plans and an opt-in CPU/Vulkan gate on an RTX 5070 Ti, while distinguishing those claims from cross-device bit identity.
The source is Apache-2.0, while model weights and converted style distributions retain NVIDIA Open Model License conditions.
demonstrates: The checked-in tree contains native inference, model conversion, validation, C ABI headers, Go bindings, a Three.js viewer, tests, parity fixtures, and optional SONIC and MuJoCo paths rather than only a concept or video.
The documented high-level controller accepts style, movement, facing, target speed or position, and seed, and returns root translations plus local rotations for a 34-joint skeleton.
The build can disable model downloads and GGML for source-only or validation subsets; normal configuration otherwise downloads and SHA-256-verifies a published 0.73 GB G1 F32 bundle and styles.
implementationContains: Strict GGUF loading, root and duration planning, pose-token prediction, VQ decoding, feature conversion, style alignment, seam blending, and skeletal-motion output.
A fixed-width C ABI with opaque handles, status returns, caller-provided error buffers, and no C++ exceptions crossing the boundary.
CPU runtime dispatch, Vulkan selection, Go PureGo bindings, a local WebSocket and Three.js demo, deterministic diagnostic sampling, and optional SONIC plus MuJoCo control.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of the supplied repository as an Aralia-relevant candidate-motion sidecar, not a general replacement animation runtime.
facts: motion-bricks.cpp is a public C++23 and GGML port of NVIDIA MotionBricks created on 2026-09-02 and inspected at main commit 2727a456e0a99baf64476496cd58115fef717944 from 2026-09-10.
The released G1 path produces root translations and local rotations for a fixed 34-joint G1 skeleton at 30 FPS from sparse constraints and controller inputs.
CPU and Vulkan share the public API; the repository also contains optional SONIC policy inference, MuJoCo physics, Go PureGo bindings, and a Three.js diagnostic viewer.
The normal configuration downloads and verifies approximately 0.73 GB of model and style assets; source-only and model-download-disabled configurations are documented.
Repository source is Apache-2.0, while the model and converted style distributions remain under NVIDIA Open Model License conditions.
The pinned head reports Linux x86-64 validation; no Windows build, browser integration, or Aralia-specific result was assessed.

Aralia currently uses project-owned browser TypeScript and Three.js animation surfaces, CC0 animation packs, multiple humanoid and creature rigs, and deterministic visual and runtime acceptance rather than a G1 native inference runtime.
The Aralia committed baseline is dff21bbc292bc508a686979180373c3bbfa86953, while the shared checkout contained 1009 tracked and untracked entries during this assessment.
inferences: The strongest fit is offline generation of candidate humanoid transition clips behind a narrow adapter, followed by ordinary retargeting and review.
The fixed G1 skeleton and native model runtime make direct browser-game integration substantially riskier than a disposable sidecar that emits a project-owned interchange format.
The explicit C ABI, error buffers, seeded controls, and parity fixtures provide useful design evidence even if no external code or weights are adopted.
Its recent creation date and fast-moving native, model, and physics surface justify a promising assessment with medium rather than high confidence.
unknowns: The repository, model bundle, styles, demo, CPU backend, Vulkan backend, SONIC path, and MuJoCo path were not downloaded, built, or run in this assessment.
No evidence shows acceptable Windows support, WebAssembly feasibility, browser bundle size, startup latency, or production frame cost for Aralia.
Retargeting quality from G1Skeleton34 to Aralia humanoids, short races, non-humanoids, equipment-bearing characters, and procedural rigs is unknown.
The legal and distribution implications of NVIDIA's model licence for generated motion, converted styles, cached weights, and an Aralia development tool have not been approved.
No same-input comparison exists against Aralia's current CC0 clips, retargeting, blending, procedural animation, or manual authoring workflows.
recommendations: Keep the repository as research evidence and do not clone, download models, add native dependencies, or change production animation behavior without a separate approved experiment.
If evaluated, start with stateless or stateful MotionBricks only; exclude SONIC, MuJoCo, robotics control, and runtime gameplay integration.

Define a project-owned candidate-motion interchange contract before execution, including skeleton mapping, units, coordinate system, frame rate, provenance, seed, model revision, and rejection evidence.
Require licensing review and a pinned source and model receipt before acquiring the model bundle.

records.title: CUDA-authored WebGPU procedural portrait with strand hair
records.summary: A public MIT implementation that deforms a CC0 MakeHuman anatomical mesh, grows up to 100,000 scalp-conforming hair strands, and shades procedural skin, iris, and sclera detail from CUDA C++ source compiled to WGSL in the browser. It is a real-time close-up portrait renderer with honest stress-test receipts, not a scan, a photoreal claim, or a Three.js material. Aralia renders stylized low-poly figures through Three.js with WebGL by default, so the direct value is a reference for GPU strand hair, footprint-filtered detail, and evidence discipline rather than a drop-in character surface.
records.problem: Render a convincing close-up human face, eyes, and hair in the browser in real time without photographic textures, scanned heads, neural rendering, or proprietary character assets, while keeping the pipeline inspectable and measurable.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of DERMIS as a distinct browser portrait-rendering identity. The evidence proves a public MIT implementation, CC0 asset provenance, a green CI run, and a working hosted demo, but no performance measurement, no Three.js integration path, and a style that differs from Aralia's stylized figures.
facts: The supplied post was published on 2026-09-16 and links a public GitHub repository and a GitHub Pages demo; the repository was created the same morning and has two commits.
The application is MIT licensed, vendors an MIT CUDA WebShader snapshot, declares no npm dependencies, and derives its anatomy from documented CC0 MakeHuman files with a rebuild script.

Three CUDA kernels deform the rest mesh and eyelids, derive normals on the GPU, trace scalp-conforming strands, evaluate pore, pigment, iris, and sclera detail, and shade with a screen-space diffusion approximation.

The README declares presets from 4,500 to 100,000 strands, 24-sample convergence for stationary views, and a 15-second to 5-minute stress test that exports JSON; it also declares that hosted CI does not test on hardware GPUs.
The hosted demo initialized in an isolated WebGPU-capable browser pane on the assessment machine and reported an active pipeline; no frame time, memory, or image quality was measured.
The v1.0.0 release publishes a 73.5 MB capture, a 4.2 MB static application ZIP, and a look preset; none were downloaded.

Aralia at the baseline pins three ^0.172.0, renders WebGL by default, exposes a WebGPU battle-map path only behind ?gpu=1 with no fallback, and builds entities from low-poly procedural parts with MeshStandardMaterial and MeshToonMaterial, including hair as authored tufts and beard wedges.
The author is the same account that publishes the threepp sample repository already retained under IB-0001.
No repository, release, asset, compiler, dependency, account, or credential entered Aralia during this assessment.
inferences: The most transferable ideas are GPU-generated scalp-conforming strand geometry, pixel-footprint filtering of fine detail to reduce shimmer, and the stress-test JSON receipt pattern, not the CUDA authoring path itself.
The CUDA-to-WGSL compiler is an authoring convenience for the author; Aralia has no CUDA source and would gain nothing from adopting that layer over direct WGSL or Three.js TSL nodes.

A photoreal-leaning portrait conflicts with Aralia's stylized, sheet-distance readability, so any use would be a separate close-up or Character Atelier portrait lane rather than a battle-map material.
Because the raster bridge and compute shading bypass Three.js materials, integration would mean a separate render pass or a re-expression of the ideas in Three.js, not a library import.

Medium confidence reflects that the implementation, licences, CI, and demo were verified, while performance, memory, and visual quality on Aralia hardware and the correctness of the vendored compiler were not.
unknowns: Frame time, GPU memory, and startup compile time at each preset on Aralia's target hardware, and behavior on integrated GPUs, are unmeasured.
Whether the strand and detail approaches survive translation to Three.js WebGPURenderer node materials without the custom raster bridge is untested.
The supported CUDA subset, correctness, and maintenance status of the vendored compiler snapshot were not inspected.
How the head mesh, expression targets, and hair would connect to Aralia's skinned biped bodies, animation clips, and toon outline pass is unknown.
The 30 FPS capture does not establish sustained real-time performance at Extreme quality on any specific GPU.
recommendations: Keep DERMIS as a separate record linked to IB-0001 for the shared author and WebGPU context, IB-0003 for WebGPU surface detail, and IB-0008 for candidate character assets.
Do not clone, vendor, or import the repository, compiler, or anatomy asset into Aralia; the style and renderer boundaries make a direct import unsuitable.
If a close-up portrait lane is ever wanted, first write a one-page Aralia-owned brief that names the scene, the target hardware, and the stylization rule before any experiment.
Reassess when the author publishes hardware-specific stress reports, when Aralia flips the WebGPU battle-map default, or when a Character Atelier portrait requirement is named.

requiredInput: A subdivided anatomical rest mesh with eye-closure targets, strand root and direction data, user settings for form, pigment, roughness, diffusion, detail, iris, hair length, and breeze, plus a camera and light setup.
processingSteps: Prepare rest geometry, eyes, brows, and strand roots on the CPU; deform the mesh and fibers with GPU kernels; derive normals on the GPU; rasterize positions and normals through a small WebGPU bridge; evaluate pore, pigment, iris, and sclera detail with footprint filtering; shade with approximate diffusion and strand highlights; accumulate samples over frames.
producedOutput: A real-time portrait image with diagnostic views, an optional 1080p WebM capture, and JSON stress-test reports with FPS, render milliseconds, and buffer size.
dependencies: A WebGPU-enabled browser, the vendored CUDA WebShader compiler and runtime, Node 20 or later for the local server and tests, and optionally Playwright with a WebGPU-capable browser for GPU tests.
runtimeRequirements: WebGPU on HTTPS or localhost with hardware acceleration and enough GPU memory for the chosen preset; the README says performance and memory depend on the device.
manualWork: Author the CUDA kernels, tune landmarks and proportions, choose presets and looks, run and read stress reports, and record showcases.
componentTypes: Authored procedural geometry and shading, deterministic GPU compute, CC0 scanned-derived base anatomy, and manual look selection; no learned components.
externalRequirements: None at runtime beyond a WebGPU browser; the compiler is bundled and the assets are local.
licenceConstraints: MIT covers the application and compiler snapshot; the anatomy is CC0 with documented derivation; the capture video carries no separate stated licence.
Any Aralia re-expression should credit MakeHuman CC0 derivation only if the same asset is used, and must not copy kernel source into a differently licensed module without preserving the MIT notice.
knownLimitations: The author states that skin diffusion is an artistic screen-space approximation, that the eyes lack physical corneal refraction, and that hosted CI does not test on hardware GPUs.
The renderer targets a single static portrait with no body, rig, clothing system, or animation clips.
doesNotSolve: Stylized rendering, full-body characters, skeletal animation, gameplay state, glTF interchange, WebGL fallback, Three.js material integration, or Aralia visual verdicts.

comparisons.externalApproach: A twice-subdivided CC0 anatomical mesh deformed on the GPU, with per-pixel procedural pore, pigment, iris, and sclera detail filtered by pixel footprint and shaded by compute kernels.
comparisons.projectApproach: Aralia assembles low-poly procedural parts such as cones and lofts with palette skin colors through MeshStandardMaterial and MeshToonMaterial, tuned for readability at sheet distance, on a skinned biped that draws in two calls.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: DERMIS spends its budget on a single close-up face; Aralia spends its budget on many readable figures at distance.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: The surface approach cannot replace Aralia's battle-map figures; it could only inform a separate close-up portrait surface if one is ever wanted.
comparisons.evidence: dermis-cuda README, human.cu and realism.cu headers, and Aralia headParts.ts, assembleEntity.ts, and material usage counts inspected 2026-09-21.
comparisons.uncertainty: No side-by-side render exists, and the visual cost of adding a close-up lane to Aralia's toon pipeline is unmeasured.

comparisons.externalApproach: Up to 100,000 individual scalp-conforming strands traced by a GPU kernel from exact scalp roots, with length and breeze controls and directional strand highlights.
comparisons.projectApproach: Aralia authors hair as solid tufts, lofts, and beard wedges in the procedural part library, colored to separate from skin at sheet distance.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: Strand hair gives close-up realism and motion; authored tufts give silhouette readability and near-zero cost.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: Strand hair would matter only for portraits; its GPU generation pattern is the reusable idea, and any test must measure it on Aralia hardware first.
comparisons.evidence: generateFibers kernel header and preset table versus organicParts.ts and headParts.ts inspected 2026-09-21.
comparisons.uncertainty: Strand cost at each preset on the target GPUs, and whether Three.js line or instanced geometry could carry the same idea, are untested.

comparisons.externalApproach: CUDA C++ compiled to WGSL at runtime by a vendored compiler, executed through a custom WebGPU raster bridge and compute shading; WebGPU is required with no fallback.
comparisons.projectApproach: Three.js r172 with WebGL by default; an opt-in WebGPURenderer battle-map path behind ?gpu=1 that fails loudly without WebGPU, using TSL node materials for terrain and grid.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: DERMIS bypasses a scene-graph renderer entirely; Aralia stays inside Three.js and expresses GPU work as node materials.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: Any Aralia use would re-express the ideas in TSL or WGSL, not adopt the CUDA layer or the bridge.
comparisons.evidence: dermis-cuda README, bridge.js and engine.js listing, THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md, and Aralia webgpuBattleMapFlag.ts inspected 2026-09-21.
comparisons.uncertainty: The vendored compiler's supported CUDA subset and correctness were not inspected.

comparisons.externalApproach: Hash manifest, documented CC0 derivation with rebuild script, third-party notices, timed stress tests with JSON reports, unit and server tests in CI, and explicit disclaimers about approximations and untested GPU CI.
comparisons.projectApproach: Aralia requires source provenance, structural tests, capture-based visual verdicts, explicit ownership, and reversible candidate promotion before any asset or technique is accepted.

records.title: GPU XPBD cloth with bone-local SDF colliders for skinned bodies
records.summary: A public Blender 5.2 add-on whose core is a Rust and WGSL compute engine: XPBD distance and bend constraints solved in parallel through Welsh-Powell graph coloring, sphere, capsule, plane and triangle mesh colliders with friction, a bone-local signed distance field baked from a skinned body into a 3D brick atlas with per-bone dirty re-bake, a hybrid joint mesh, layer ids with thickness, GPU spatial-hash self collision, edge collision and adaptive substeps. The engine crate is public domain; the Blender side is GPL. Aralia has no runtime cloth and renders skinned Character Atelier bodies with script-authored garments through Three.js WebGL, so the direct value is the collision and layering design, not the add-on. A sibling project (Wildkin) ported the bone SDF, the edge collision and the layer rule to a CPU solver and measured them: the SDF was rejected, the other two work.
records.problem: Keep fitted garments outside a posed skinned body, outside the garment under them and under the garment over them while the body moves, at interactive rates, without an offline drape per body.

sources.title: TareminCloth repository
sources.licence: The Unlicense (public domain) for crates/cloth_core and crates/cloth_gui; Unlicense OR GPL-3.0-or-later for crates/cloth_py; GPL-3.0-or-later for __init__.py and python/ (the Blender add-on); the GitHub API reports the repository licence as Other because the LICENSE file is a multi-licence notice
sources.provenance: The repository was cloned read-only on 2026-09-20 into the separate Wildkin repository at research/taremin-cloth/upstream (a shallow clone of the then default-branch head 901b8a0), outside Aralia. Nothing was built, installed or run; Blender was not started. Every file under crates/cloth_core/src was read, plus the LICENSE, README, Cargo and pyproject files and the Python presets, properties, runner and collider modules named in the map. Repository metadata, the release list and the current head were read through the GitHub API on 2026-09-22; the head had moved to a7166d8 (2026-09-22T06:17:28Z, a smoothing brush) and that later work was not inspected. The comments and README are Japanese and were read directly.
claims: The README describes a Blender 5.2 LTS add-on with a GPU XPBD cloth solver in Rust and WGSL bound through PyO3, Welsh-Powell colored constraint projection, distance and dihedral bending constraints, pinning, seam sewing, interactive grab, sphere, capsule, plane and mesh colliders with friction, a bone-local SDF collider baked into a 3D brick atlas in about 0.1 s, a fully GPU dynamic re-bake of only the bones whose pose changed at 70 FPS or more, a hybrid joint mesh over about 10 to 15 percent of the body, a single-mesh box SDF with a VRAM budget, multi-layer clothing by layer id and thickness, self collision, fabric, quality and collider presets, and backend and device selection.
The README claims stable collision under animation with only 4x4 bone matrices uploaded per frame.
demonstrates: The crate holds 20 WGSL compute shaders (predict, colored distance, atomic Jacobi distance, bending, sewing, pin, collision, edge collision, four self-collision stages, spatial grid sort, normals, velocity update, skinning, bone triangle preparation, bone SDF bake and mesh SDF bake), a coloring module, a spatial hash builder, an SDF baker, a debug recorder and a simulation module with a shader alignment test suite.

The bending constraint in the code is a distance constraint between the two vertices opposite an interior edge (crates/cloth_core/src/mesh.rs:367-409, shaders/bending.wgsl:84-91), not a dihedral angle constraint as the README says.

Multiple bone fields combine by plain minimum (shaders/collision.wgsl:236-242); a smooth-minimum helper exists but is never called, and the blend_k slot in the bone info actually carries the weight threshold (src/sdf_baker.rs:285).
The adaptive substep rule (a CFL bound on the last displacement with hysteresis) lives in the GPL Python runner (python/taremin_cloth/engine/runner.py:161-231), not in the public-domain crate.
A single v0.0.1 release from 2026-09-18 publishes Windows, Linux and macOS zips; the repository had 12 stars, 0 forks and 1 open issue on 2026-09-22.
implementationContains: A complete GPU cloth engine (Rust, wgpu, WGSL) with mesh preparation, constraint coloring, SDF baking, a spatial hash, recording and tests; a PyO3 binding crate; a native review GUI crate; and a Blender add-on in Python with panels, properties, presets, a simulation runner, a collider bridge with a per-bone dirty list and joint-region extraction, and CLI log tools.
It contains no browser or WebGPU path, no Three.js or glTF integration, no runtime game loop and no fitting of garments to bodies; garments enter as Blender meshes already placed on the body.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment. The engine crate is public domain and was read in full. In the separate Wildkin project its bone-local SDF collider, its edge collision and its layer rule were ported to a CPU JavaScript solver and measured on a fitted tunic and trousers over two skinned bodies: the bind-pose bone SDF was rejected (it becomes a rigid wall where bones blend), edge collision removed about 40 percent of the remaining skin crossings at 8 to 15 ms per model, and the layer rule kept the tunic outside the trousers and under the belt at 1.2 to 1.6 ms per model. Aralia has no runtime cloth requirement today, so the record is a watch item with a bounded experiment for the Character Atelier.
facts: The repository was created on 2026-09-18, has one release (v0.0.1, 2026-09-18) and was at commit 901b8a0 (2026-09-19) when cloned read-only into the Wildkin repository on 2026-09-20; the head had moved to a7166d8 by 2026-09-22.

crates/cloth_core and crates/cloth_gui are released under The Unlicense; crates/cloth_py is Unlicense OR GPL-3.0-or-later; the Blender add-on Python is GPL-3.0-or-later (LICENSE, pyproject.toml:11, each Cargo.toml).

The solver runs one substep loop per frame (predict, then per iteration pin, colored distance, colored sewing, colored bending and collision, then a final pin pass, edge collision, self collision, optional relaxation and velocity update; crates/cloth_core/src/simulation/dispatch.rs:7-208). Substep count, gravity and the time step come from Python; adaptive substeps use a CFL bound on the last frame displacement with a rise limit of 4 and a fall limit of 2 per frame (python/taremin_cloth/engine/runner.py:161-231).

Constraints are Welsh-Powell colored on shared vertices; each color is one dispatch; an atomic Jacobi path with over-relaxation 1.25 is the fallback (src/coloring.rs, shaders/distance_atomic.wgsl:131).

The bone SDF bake assigns a triangle to a bone when any vertex has nonzero weight for it and its box overlaps the bone box padded by 20 percent plus thickness, stores signed distance and interpolated bone weight as two f16 per voxel in a brick atlas, and at run time samples each candidate bone trilinearly, masks samples with weight under the threshold, takes the closest bone and pushes along the central-difference gradient (src/sdf_baker.rs:167-365, shaders/bake_sdf.wgsl:90-148, shaders/collision.wgsl:115-252). The dynamic mode re-skins the body on the GPU and re-bakes only dirty bones and their dependents (src/simulation/mod.rs:1257-1301, python/taremin_cloth/engine/collider.py:671-687).

Layering: the contact distance between cloth vertices is the sum of their thicknesses and only the higher layer id moves; the escape push fires only for the higher layer (shaders/self_collision_solve_vt.wgsl:250-252, shaders/self_collision.wgsl:347-371).

Wildkin measurement, 2026-09-20 (Wildkin research/taremin-cloth/README.md section 5): the bind-pose bone SDF, ported to CPU typed arrays at 10 mm voxels, matched the skin in the bind pose with 0 strain violations where capsules gave 64 to 91, but in the standing pose and at full elbow bend it pushed the collar to 13.9x and the sleeve to 3.5x to 5.2x strain against 2.7x and 1.3x to 1.7x without it, cost 12 to 28 ms per model per frame plus a 2.5 to 3.3 s bake, and added texture stretch on the tunic (158 and 127 faces newly over 2:1 against 94 and 65).

Wildkin measurement, 2026-09-22 (same README, section 5b): edge midpoints tested against the skin before the final vertex pass removed about 40 percent of the crossing faces the vertex solver left (26 to 16 in the stance armpit, 55 to 38 and 74 to 48 at full bend) with 0 vertices inside the skin and no added strain, at 8 to 15 ms per model per frame; the layer rule moved 20 tunic vertices out of the trousers and 35 to 62 from above the belt every frame at 1.2 to 1.6 ms with no strain or texture change. Both stay behind checkboxes, off by default.

Aralia at the baseline pins three ^0.172.0, renders WebGL by default with an opt-in WebGPU battle-map path, and ships fourteen skinned Character Atelier GLB models built from CC0 MakeHuman anatomy with script-authored garments baked at export (docs/architecture/domains/character-creator.md); no Aralia source simulates cloth at run time.
No repository, release, binary, package or asset entered Aralia during this assessment; the read-only clone lives in the Wildkin repository.
inferences: The reusable ideas for a skinned-body project are the collision and layering rules, not the GPU engine: a bind-pose per-bone field is a worse body proxy than the posed triangles a CPU solver can already query, which is why the source needs its dynamic re-bake and its joint mesh; edge collision and the layer id plus thickness rule transfer directly and cheaply.

The public-domain core makes porting and copying of the engine math free of licence work; only the Blender Python (presets, adaptive substeps, the dirty bone list) is GPL and must be re-expressed rather than copied.
The README overstates two points that the code does not support: the bending constraint is not dihedral, and bone fields are not smoothly blended. Assessments should cite the code, not the README.

For Aralia the technique matters only if a Character Atelier garment must stay outside a posed body at run time; today the garments are baked into the export and no such requirement is named, so the record is a watch item.

Medium confidence reflects a full read of the crate and a measured port of three of its designs in a sibling project, against no run of the add-on, no GPU timing of the source and no Aralia experiment.
unknowns: The add-on was not run, so its 0.1 s bake, 70 FPS dynamic re-bake and self-collision behavior are README claims, not measurements.
Whether the GPU engine would port to Three.js WebGPURenderer and TSL, and at what cost per body, is untested; the Wildkin numbers are CPU numbers.
How the layer rule behaves with armor pieces and rigid attachments, and how the source handles garments that must be under a rigid piece, was not exercised.
The later commits after 901b8a0 (a smoothing brush and anything else) were not inspected.
Whether the Wildkin repository is the saved D&D Character Generator project listed on this board is unconfirmed.
recommendations: Keep this record linked to IB-0010 (MakeHuman-derived bodies, WebGPU context) and IB-0008 (candidate character assets); do not import the add-on, its binaries or the crate into Aralia.
If a Character Atelier garment ever needs to follow a posed body at run time, start from the Wildkin CPU solver record and its layer rule, not from a WebGPU port of this engine.
Cite the shader and Rust line references in Wildkin research/taremin-cloth/README.md section 2 rather than the source README for any design claim.
Reassess when Aralia names a runtime garment requirement, when the author publishes measured bake and frame numbers, or when Aralia flips its WebGPU default.

requiredInput: A cloth mesh placed on the body in Blender (object space), colliders in world space (analytic shapes, triangle meshes, or a skinned body with bone matrices and weights), per-vertex pins and layer ids, fabric and quality presets, gravity and the frame time step.
processingSteps: Weld and color the constraints on the CPU; per substep on the GPU: predict with gravity and damping, project pin, distance, sewing and bending constraints color by color, collide against analytic shapes, mesh triangles with continuous collision and the bone SDF atlas, collide edges, resolve self collision through a spatial hash with relief and step clamps, relax, update velocities; in dynamic mode skin the body on the GPU and re-bake the dirty bone fields first.
producedOutput: Updated cloth vertex positions per frame read back into Blender, optional shape keys or baked timeline, a JSONL debug recording, and rendered review images from the CLI tools.
dependencies: Blender 5.2 LTS, Rust 1.80 or later to build, wgpu with a Vulkan, DirectX 12 or Metal device, PyO3 ABI3, Python 3 for the add-on and tools.
runtimeRequirements: A desktop GPU driver with compute support and VRAM for the SDF atlas (a 256 MB default budget with automatic resolution fit); Blender running; no browser path.
manualWork: Place and enable the cloth and colliders in Blender, pick presets, pin vertices, set layer ids and thickness, choose the SDF mode and resolution, and review results in the viewport or the log tools.
componentTypes: Deterministic GPU compute (XPBD), CPU preprocessing (welding, coloring, SDF layout), authored presets and settings; no learned components.
externalRequirements: None at run time beyond Blender and a GPU; the release zips bundle the compiled core.
licenceConstraints: The engine crate and the WGSL shaders are public domain (The Unlicense) and may be copied or ported into any project with or without attribution.
The Blender add-on Python is GPL-3.0-or-later; its adaptive substep rule, presets and dirty-bone logic may be described and re-expressed but not copied into non-GPL code.
knownLimitations: The bone SDF is rigid per bone; the source itself adds a joint mesh and a dynamic re-bake because the field is wrong where bones blend.
The bending constraint is an opposite-vertex distance, not a dihedral angle; bone fields combine by minimum, not a smooth blend.
Cloth enters in object space and colliders in world space with no compensating transform in the code that was read.
doesNotSolve: Fitting a garment to a body, garment construction, browser or game-engine integration, glTF export of simulated results, or any rendering.

comparisons.externalApproach: XPBD with separate tension and compression compliance, shear edges, opposite-vertex bending, sewing and pins, many substeps per frame with adaptive count, gravity and velocities, all on the GPU in colored dispatches.
comparisons.projectApproach: Aralia has no runtime cloth. Character Atelier garments are script-authored in MakeHuman, baked into skinned GLB exports and follow the skeleton by skinning only.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: The source simulates cloth dynamics; Aralia deforms garments by skin weights and accepts the result at export.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: Nothing in the solver model can be adopted until Aralia states a runtime garment requirement; the Wildkin sibling project shows that a position-based correction of the skinned pose, without gravity or substeps, is enough to keep a fitted garment outside a posed body.
comparisons.evidence: crates/cloth_core/src/simulation/dispatch.rs:7-208 and shaders/distance.wgsl:76-96 at 901b8a0; docs/architecture/domains/character-creator.md and scripts/character-atelier/build_characters.py at the Aralia baseline; Wildkin reviews/base-rig-m5/RUNTIME-CLOTH.md.
comparisons.uncertainty: No Aralia model was posed against a solver, so the size of any garment-through-body defect in Character Atelier exports is unmeasured.

comparisons.externalApproach: Per-bone signed distance fields in a brick atlas, sampled trilinearly with a bone-weight mask, closest bone by minimum, re-baked per dirty bone from the GPU-skinned body, plus a partial triangle mesh at joints.
comparisons.projectApproach: None at run time; at export the garment is fitted to the rest body once. The Wildkin sibling solver queries the posed skin triangles directly through a grid every frame.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: A field is cheap to sample and needs a re-bake to follow the pose; the posed triangles are exact and need no bake.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: Measured in Wildkin: the bind-pose field pushed the collar to 13.9x strain and cost 12 to 28 ms per model; the posed-triangle pass held the same gap with no such strain. A field only pays off with the GPU re-bake the source has.
comparisons.evidence: shaders/collision.wgsl:115-252, src/sdf_baker.rs:167-365 and src/simulation/mod.rs:1257-1301 at 901b8a0; Wildkin research/taremin-cloth/README.md section 5.
comparisons.uncertainty: The source dynamic mode was not run, so its 70 FPS claim with re-bake is unverified.

comparisons.externalApproach: Layer id plus thickness: only the higher layer moves at a contact; edge segments are tested against faces and face corners against edges so a chord cannot sag through a surface.
comparisons.projectApproach: Aralia bakes garment order at export and has no runtime layer or edge test. The Wildkin sibling solver adopted both rules on the CPU on 2026-09-22.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: Both rules are independent of the GPU engine and of the solver model.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: These are the two designs worth carrying into any skinned-garment runtime: measured in Wildkin at 1.2 to 1.6 ms (layers) and 8 to 15 ms (edges) per model per frame on the CPU, with no added strain or texture stretch.
comparisons.evidence: shaders/self_collision_solve_vt.wgsl:250-252, shaders/self_collision.wgsl:347-371 and shaders/edge_collision.wgsl:141-376 at 901b8a0; Wildkin research/taremin-cloth/README.md section 5b.
comparisons.uncertainty: Edge collision in a folded crease halves the remaining crossings but does not clear them within the strain limit; behavior with rigid armor pieces is untested.

comparisons.externalApproach: Blender add-on, Rust and WGSL through wgpu, PyO3 binding; the engine public domain, the add-on GPL.
comparisons.projectApproach: Three.js r172 in the browser, WebGL by default, opt-in WebGPU battle map; assets and code owned by Aralia with provenance rules.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: No shared runtime; the shader math is free to port, the Python rules are not free to copy.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: Any Aralia use is a re-expression in JavaScript or TSL owned by Aralia, as Wildkin did in CPU JavaScript with a header attribution.

lexicon.meaning: Extended position-based dynamics. A stable cloth solver that moves vertices to satisfy constraints each substep instead of integrating forces.
The two constraint types that keep cloth edges at rest length and resist folding.
Grouping constraints so no two in a group share a vertex. Each group can then solve in parallel on the GPU. Welsh-Powell is the ordering heuristic used.
A Rust implementation of the WebGPU API that runs on native GPUs. Here it executes the WGSL compute kernels inside Blender.
WebGPU Shading Language. The language of the compute kernels.
SDF. A 3D grid that stores the distance to the nearest surface, negative inside. Cloth reads it to push out of the body.
An SDF baked per bone in that bone's own space, so it follows a skinned body without a re-bake every frame.
A 3D texture that packs many small SDF blocks, with a lookup table from bone to block.
A grid-based lookup that finds nearby vertices quickly, used for self collision.
Each garment layer has an order and a thickness, so an outer layer stays outside an inner one.
Smaller time steps inside one frame. Adaptive substeps add more when motion is fast.
A public-domain dedication for the engine crate. The Blender add-on side is GPL, which needs separate review.
A sibling project that ported parts of this design to a CPU solver and measured them.

records.title: Durable personal-agent application with reviewed actions and an isolated agent computer
records.summary: OpenMuse is an MIT alpha from CopilotKit: a personal agent with a chat client, a server-owned durable task engine, stored action reviews with receipts, a persistent Chromium browser worker with human takeover, and an optional network-less Docker Linux computer. It streams AG-UI events through the CopilotKit runtime and targets iOS, Android, and web through Expo. Aralia is a game, not an assistant product, so the value is in the operational patterns for Aralia's own agent tooling: SQL-leased durable work, approval bound to reviewed content, honest uncertain outcomes, and a bounded agent computer. Live model, Google, and Rich Threads acceptance are explicitly pending upstream.
records.problem: Let a person delegate open-ended work to an agent that can browse, run commands, and act on external accounts, while every external action is reviewed, every outcome is recorded, interrupted work recovers, and the agent's computer cannot reach the host.
