lexicon.meaning: An open-source framework for agent chat interfaces and runtimes. OpenMuse is built on it and by the same company.
Agent-User Interaction protocol. A stream of typed events between an agent runtime and a client, such as messages, tool calls, and state.
A separate hosted CopilotKit service for conversation persistence and replay. It needs a project key and is not part of the MIT repository.
A server-owned job with a plan, checkpoints, and saved outcomes that survives restarts and can pause, resume, cancel, or retry.
A time-limited claim on a task stored in the database. If a worker dies, the lease expires and another worker recovers the task.
A stored approval that binds one proposed external action to the account, the exact reviewed content, and the provider version before it is sent.
The saved record of what an action or command did, including uncertain outcomes that need reconciliation.
A separate token-protected Playwright Chromium service with persistent profiles that the agent drives and the person can take over.
Opening the agent's live browser session so the person continues the work by hand.
OpenMuse's name for the persistent browser plus the optional Docker Linux container with files and a terminal.
An embedded PostgreSQL that runs inside the Node process. It cannot be shared between processes.
A small web framework for the API server.
The toolchain that builds one client for iOS, Android, and web.
A separate CopilotKit agent backend. OpenMuse ships a disabled, contract-tested adapter for it.
Aralia's own agent coordination daemon and orchestrator: a store of agents, locks, tasks, and messages with an SSE dashboard.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of OpenMuse as a distinct durable personal-agent application identity. The evidence proves a candid MIT alpha with a broad test suite and green CI, but its product is an assistant, not a game, and its live model, Google, and Rich Threads acceptance are pending. The value for Aralia is in agent-tooling patterns, not the application.
facts: The repository was created on 2026-09-15 under the MIT licence, had 822 stars and 84 forks at inspection, and its head commit 82ff35b9 from 2026-09-22 passed CI.

The architecture is an Expo client, a Hono API with the CopilotKit runtime and AG-UI streaming, a durable task worker coordinated by SQL leases over PGlite or PostgreSQL, a Playwright browser worker, and an optional Docker Linux computer.

The security policy states concrete container limits: nonroot, read-only root, no capabilities, no network, 512 MB, one CPU, a 30-second command timeout, and no host shell fallback; it also states the browser worker is not a hostile-tenant boundary.
External writes require a stored approval bound to reviewed content and provider version; uncertain outcomes are retained and never replayed automatically.

The verification notes report 154 passing tests, a real Chromium lifecycle test, and a real Docker smoke test on 2026-09-16, and state that live model, Google, Rich Threads, and Android device acceptance remain pending.
Live deployments require a CopilotKit Intelligence project key for Rich Threads; that service is hosted and outside the MIT licence.

Aralia at the baseline runs its own agent tooling: the Agora coordination daemon with a store, bearer tokens, locks, tasks, heartbeat leases, and an SSE dashboard; an orchestrator that dispatches waves and gates them; a multi-session PTY manager that runs agents directly on the host; and a separate operator dashboard repository, because AGENTS.md keeps the control plane out of the game.
The Idea Board itself gained a browser-local Remember page on 2026-09-22 for personal idea capture, which is a small parallel to OpenMuse's Ideas and memory surfaces.
No repository, package, model key, Google account, CopilotKit project, container, or production state entered Aralia during this assessment.
inferences: The transferable value is four operational patterns: server-owned durable work with SQL leases, approval bound to a content hash and provider version, honest uncertain-outcome receipts with no hidden retry, and a network-less container for agent commands.
Aralia's Agora already has leases, locks, and tokens, but its agents run as host PTY sessions with full shell access; the OpenMuse container boundary is the largest gap between the two.
The client stack, Google adapters, PDF and finance features, and Rich Threads are irrelevant to Aralia and would bring a hosted dependency.
Because Aralia keeps its control plane in a separate repository, any pattern adoption belongs there or in tools/agora, never in the game source.
Medium confidence reflects that the code structure, tests, policies, and CI were verified through the API, while no test was run and no behavior was observed.
unknowns: Whether the lease, approval, and receipt implementations are cleanly separable from CopilotKit runtime types, or entangled with the client protocol.
Actual reliability of lease recovery, review binding, and container limits under load; the authors' tests were not run here.
How OpenMuse behaves with a live model on open-ended tasks; the authors list this as pending.
Whether Aralia's operator dashboard owners want approval gating for agent actions at all, given the current human-in-chat model.
The pace and direction of the project; eight commits in one day were documentation changes, and the OpenBot bridge is unbuilt.
recommendations: Keep OpenMuse as a separate record linked to IB-0006 and IB-0008, the two records where agents drive tools through MCP, and do not open a record per CopilotKit product.
Do not clone, install, or vendor OpenMuse or CopilotKit into Aralia or its operator dashboard; the assistant product and the hosted Intelligence service do not fit.

If the Agora owners want stronger action gating, write a one-page Aralia-owned design for a stored approval receipt on mutating orchestrator endpoints, informed by the OpenMuse security policy, before any code.
Reassess when the authors publish live-model and Google acceptance, when Aralia moves agent sessions into containers, or when a control-plane owner names a gating requirement.

records.title: CC0 universal humanoid animation library for retargeting
records.summary: Quaternius's Universal Animation Library is a hand-authored pack of more than 120 humanoid animations on one universal rig, released under CC0, with a free Standard download, paid Pro and Blender Source tiers, and root-motion and in-place variants. Aralia already retargets a CC0 Mesh2Motion clip pack onto its 17-bone biped with rotation-only, in-place clips, so this library could slot into that existing boundary as a second clip source. The pack was not downloaded; its bone names, clip quality, and fit to Aralia's proportions are unverified.
records.problem: Give every generated humanoid a broad, legally clean set of locomotion, combat, emote, and death clips without commissioning mocap or hand-keying each motion, while keeping Aralia's own skeleton and gait system authoritative.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment of the Quaternius Universal Animation Library as a distinct authored CC0 clip-library identity. The licence and the fit to Aralia's existing CC0 retarget boundary are strong, but the files were not downloaded, so bone mapping and clip quality are unverified.
facts: The supplied post from 2025-03-19 announces the library and links its itch.io page.
The store page states CC0, more than 120 animations on one universal humanoid rig, root-motion and in-place versions, and a Blender Source tier.
The Standard tier is a 15 MB download at any price including zero; Pro and Source cost at least 9.99 and 14.99 USD.

Aralia at the baseline loads two CC0 Mesh2Motion clip packs from public/anim/humanoid, about 5.7 MB and 5.3 MB, and retargets them once onto a 17-bone biped with SkeletonUtils in world space.
Aralia's humanoidRetarget module keeps rotation tracks only and drops root translation, because its gait system moves the entity group; digit bones hold their driver pose during clips.
Aralia's 2026-05-21 3D combat map design spec already names Quaternius CC0 packs as candidate character and prop sources.
No file, account, payment, or dependency entered Aralia during this assessment.
inferences: The library fits Aralia's existing boundary well: a second CC0 pack needs only a new bone-name map into humanoidRetarget, not a new loader or runtime.
The in-place version matches Aralia's rotation-only, gait-driven model; the root-motion version adds nothing Aralia would keep.

records.title: Image-conditioned sparse mesh refinement for generated assets
records.summary: An open inference release (Hi3D v1.0, built on Sparc3D) that takes a coarse mesh plus one reference image of the same object and refines the geometry through up to three sparse passes with 512, 1024 and 1536 cubed extraction grids. The code and eight weight files are public under the Hi3D Open License Agreement 1.0: commercial use is permitted, products that embed the model must carry a badge and apply for a separate licence above a scale threshold, while standalone output meshes carry no such obligation. It is geometry only, Linux and CUDA only, and validated solely on a 96 GB GPU, so it does not fit the hero pipeline’s 24 GB L4 job today.
records.problem: Sharpen the soft geometry that image-to-3D generators leave on Aralia’s hero creatures and props (today TRELLIS.2 masters) without hand sculpting, while keeping every generator a detached candidate stage that never touches runtime assets.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment from the public repository at a pinned commit; the supplied X article itself was not readable from the assessing session. The release is real, documented, and permissive for output meshes, but its GPU floor and geometry-only output keep it out of the current hero pipeline until a smaller-card feasibility result and a texture-restoration step exist.

projectBaseline.dirtyNote: Clean cloud clone of branch ccr-2da4fbce-xouf23 at the commit named; no uncommitted work existed before this record was written.

facts: The README, read at commit 13657ad (2026-10-24), gives the release date as 2026-10-23 and describes Hi3D v1.0 as refinement of a coarse mesh into high-resolution geometry conditioned on one reference image of the same object, built on the Sparc3D representation and refinement architecture.

Three refinement passes are documented: nominal structural grids of 64, 128 and 192 cubed with sparse extraction grids of 512, 1024 and 1536 cubed; a 512 request runs one pass, 1024 two, and 1536 all three, each with 25 scheduler updates by default.

The documented Python API is Sparc3DPipeline.from_pretrained(“hi3d-official/Hi3Dv1.0”), called with a PIL image, a trimesh mesh, a resolution in {512, 1024, 1536}, a step count and a seed; it returns a geometry-only trimesh.Trimesh. demo/refine_mesh.py exposes the same with --sequential-cpu-offload, --remove-background and offline flags.
Output is geometry only: no textures, materials or vertex colours, and the mesh is recentred and normalised to unit maximum radius, so input scale and world coordinates are not preserved.

Requirements are Linux, Python 3.10 only, an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 8.0 or newer, a CUDA toolkit in the 12.0 to 12.5 range, flash-attn 2.7.4.post1 with no fallback attention path, spconv-cu120 2.3.6 and Triton kernels; there is no CPU inference path. The measured stack was Python 3.10.12, PyTorch 2.5.0+cu124 and a 96 GB NVIDIA H20, and both docs/installation.md and docs/pipeline.md say the 1536 ladder was validated only on that GPU with no minimum VRAM established.

Weights are eight files on Hugging Face (model_index.json, a scheduler config, a VAE config and safetensors, transformer_512 and transformer_1024 configs and safetensors); the conditioning encoders facebook/dinov2-large and openai/clip-vit-large-patch14 are downloaded separately on first use. The loader reads JSON and safetensors only and does not unpickle checkpoints.

The repository holds inference code only; training code, the evaluation harness, benchmark splits and comparison meshes are not included. GPU sparse convolution and attention are stated to be not bitwise deterministic, so seeds do not act as mesh hashes.

The LICENSE is the Hi3D Open License Agreement Version 1.0 dated 2026-10-22 from OCEANO HK HOLDING LIMITED. It grants a royalty-free licence to use, modify, distribute and sell the Hi3D Materials; commercial use is permitted; a product that integrates the Materials must display “Powered by Hi3D 1.0” (Section 7); a Related Product above 200,000 monthly active users or USD 1,000,000 monthly revenue must apply for a separate licence within 60 days (Section 5); and Section 9 says outputs containing no Hi3D Materials carry none of the branding, NOTICE or scale obligations. Third-party portions keep their Apache-2.0 and MIT terms per NOTICE.

An optional demo adapter (demo/coarse_stage.py) calls Tencent Hunyuan3D-2 mini as a coarse generator; the README states Hunyuan is neither a dependency of the core library nor relicensed by Hi3D, and demo/refine_mesh.py has no Hunyuan import.

Aralia at the baseline makes hero creature masters with Microsoft TRELLIS.2: tools/creatureHero/convert.py and gcp/gcp-convert.sh run it on a self-owned GCP spot g2-standard-8 with one 24 GB NVIDIA L4 (about EUR 0.25 to 0.40 per hour, 15 to 25 minutes a run) and export a textured master.glb at a 100,000-face target with 1024-pixel textures; tools/creatureHero/optimize.mjs then reduces it to the 30,000-triangle runtime budget.
No weights were downloaded, no environment was built, and nothing was run during this assessment; no file from the release entered Aralia.
inferences: The natural slot in Aralia is a second stage between the TRELLIS.2 master export and optimize.mjs: refine the master’s geometry against the same reference.png, then re-project or re-bake the TRELLIS.2 textures, because the refiner discards them.

The hero job’s 24 GB L4 is a quarter of the only validated GPU, and the release establishes no minimum VRAM, so the existing GCP recipe cannot be assumed to host even the 512 pass; feasibility must be measured rather than inferred from the offload flag.

Licensing is favourable for Aralia’s consumption pattern: a refined mesh shipped in the game is a standalone output, so the game owes no badge; only a tool or service that embeds the model, such as a hosted Entity Studio refiner, would.
Medium confidence reflects primary documentation read at a pinned commit against a known project baseline, with no run, no output inspected, and the supplied post unread.
unknowns: Peak GPU memory of the 512 and 1024 passes on a 24 GB L4 or a 40 to 48 GB card, with and without sequential CPU offload.
Whether a TRELLIS.2 master is a suitable coarse input, since the README warns that severe structural errors persist and hidden geometry is a plausible completion.
How to restore scale and textures after refinement, because the output is renormalised and untextured; whether TRELLIS.2 UVs survive any re-projection.
Wall-clock time and cost for one creature at each resolution, and how often adaptive voxelisation downgrades the support grid or a run raises on an unreachable resolution.
What the supplied X article says beyond its indexed title, and whether the Hugging Face model card adds conditions not present in the repository.
recommendations: Keep this as a watch record; do not add Hi3D to the hero job until a smaller-card feasibility result exists.
If tested, run the official demo/refine_mesh.py on one existing hero master and its reference.png on a rented GPU of at least 80 GB first, to separate “does it help” from “does it fit the L4”.
Treat the refined mesh as a candidate under Entity Studio review with the TRELLIS.2 master as the baseline; keep optimize.mjs as the only path to runtime assets.
Keep the licence facts (outputs free, integrations badged, scale threshold) in this record rather than in code, since Aralia would only ever consume outputs.

requiredInput: One reference image of the object (PNG; alpha retained for framing, background removal optional) and one coarse mesh of the same object loadable by trimesh, plus a resolution, a step count and a seed.
processingSteps: Image features from DINOv2-large and CLIP condition sparse flow on coordinates derived from the coarse geometry; each pass samples sparse latents, decodes them with a self-pruning sparse VAE, extracts a mesh, and revoxelises it as the support for the next pass.
producedOutput: A geometry-only trimesh.Trimesh recentred to unit maximum radius, exported by the caller (the demo writes GLB), plus the achieved resolution.
dependencies: The sparc3d package from the repository, torch 2.5.0+cu124, torchvision 0.20.0, transformers 4.46 to below 5, spconv-cu120 2.3.6, flash-attn 2.7.4.post1, triton 3.1 or newer, accelerate, trimesh and pyfqmr; the eight weight files; DINOv2-large and CLIP ViT-L/14 from Hugging Face.
runtimeRequirements: Linux, Python 3.10, CUDA toolkit 12.0 to 12.5, an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 8.0 or newer with no stated minimum VRAM (only a 96 GB H20 is validated), batch size one, optional sequential CPU offload.
manualWork: Produce the coarse mesh and a matching reference, choose resolution and seed, restore scale and textures afterwards, and inspect every view of the result.
componentTypes: Learned sparse-latent diffusion refinement, learned image encoders, deterministic sparse voxelisation and FlexiCubes-style mesh extraction kernels, and a Python command-line demo.
externalRequirements: Hugging Face downloads of the weights and both encoders, a CUDA Linux host, and acceptance of the Hi3D Open License Agreement 1.0.
licenceConstraints: Hi3D Open License Agreement 1.0 on the Hi3D portions and weights: commercial use allowed; “Powered by Hi3D 1.0” required on any product or service that embeds the Materials; a separate licence required above 200,000 monthly active users or USD 1,000,000 monthly revenue; the Acceptable Use Policy passes downstream.
Standalone outputs carry none of those obligations (Section 9).
Apache-2.0 and MIT terms are retained for the Sparc3D, TRELLIS, Pointcept, O-CNN and FlexiCubes portions; Hunyuan3D-2 mini, DINOv2 and CLIP keep their own terms.
knownLimitations: Geometry only, scale not preserved, no CPU path, no fallback attention, non-deterministic on GPU, coarse structural errors persist, hidden surfaces are completions, and a run that cannot reach the requested resolution raises instead of degrading.
doesNotSolve: Coarse generation itself, texturing, materials, rigging, animation, collision, LODs, canonical scale, runtime budgets, or review and promotion into accepted Aralia assets.

comparisons.practicalConsequence: Any gain would land in the master.glb, not the runtime asset, so it matters only where the master is viewed closely or re-reduced with a better silhouette.

lexicon.meaning: A first-pass 3D shape with the right overall structure but soft or missing surface detail; the refiner’s input.
The nominal voxel resolution (512, 1024 or 1536 cubed) at which the surface is extracted; only occupied cells are stored, so it is not a dense tensor.
The decoder that turns sparse latents into surface voxels and discards cells that carry no surface.
Keeping model weights on the CPU and streaming them to the GPU as needed to lower GPU residency; it does not remove decoded-feature memory.
In the Hi3D licence, a generated mesh that contains no Hi3D code or weights; it carries none of the branding or scale obligations.

records.title: Two-camera AI video motion capture for rigged non-humanoid creatures
records.summary: AnyMove (patch-gg/anymove, Apache-2.0, v0.1.0) animates any rigged creature from one AI video: a video model films the creature from a front and a side orthographic camera in one frame, a DINOv2 joint reader trained on that one creature finds every joint in both views, shared heights pin each joint in 3D, and a forward-kinematics fit exports a rigged, animated GLB. The authors report wolf, dragon, giant spider and fire demon captures with reader errors of 3 to 9 px and a 0.94 cm exam on the wolf. It needs Blender 5.x, Python 3.11, a 24 GB CUDA GPU to train a reader, and a fal account for MiniMax H3 Max clips at about USD 0.26 each. Eight-legged walking and lying down do not fit yet.
records.problem: Give Aralia’s non-humanoid creatures real clips (idle, attack, rear, roar, wing beat) without hand animation, for a bestiary of rigged species that today can only come from Mesh2Motion’s fixed packs, while procedural gaits keep owning locomotion.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment from the repository at a pinned commit, the day the owner supplied it. The pipeline is complete, documented and permissively licensed, and its output unit (a self-contained rigged, animated GLB) is the unit the approved bestiary plan consumes, so it is promising as a third source of bestiary species. Nothing was run; the figures are the authors’ own.

projectBaseline.dirtyNote: Cloud clone of branch ccr-2da4fbce-xouf23 at the commit named, carrying the uncommitted IB-0015 board edits and a status note on the bestiary plan-map feature; no source code differed from the baseline.

facts: The repository at commit 7a82a0a (2026-10-27) is Apache-2.0 code with the Patch marks excluded; plugin.json names version 0.1.0. The README credits the two-camera method to @CanItCode (a YouTube video) and the MiniMax H3 LoRA step to @Graalitoo (an X post); neither was opened.

Pipeline per README, PIPELINE.md and the skills: a textured mesh (Tripo H3.1 on fal at USD 0.40, or any GLB) is scaled to real size facing -Y; joints are placed by hand in rig.json over grid views; Blender builds the armature with automatic weights and paints each limb its own colour; one reference image holds a front and a side orthographic view sharing the vertical axis; that image plus a strict prompt go to MiniMax H3 Max image-to-video on fal (768P, 5 s, about USD 0.26; H3, H3 Max Turbo, Seedance 2.5 and FLUX 3 Max are also wired); the reader finds joints in both views; shared heights triangulate them; a forward-kinematics fit in torch with Euler joint limits exports a GLB at 24 fps through Blender.

The joint reader is facebook/dinov2-with-registers-base (ViT-B/14, Apache-2.0) plus an upsampling heatmap head at 448 px input and 128 px heatmaps, trained per creature on about 2,200 Blender-rendered random poses inside the joint limits with known joints (half near rest, random motion blur, lights and turns): about 25 min of rendering on one RTX 4090 and 17 to 20 min of training at about 12 GB.

Capture per the anymove-capture skill: the clip is aligned to the reference frame by an ECC affine fit, split into views and read (about 10 s for 5 s of video); paw agreement is the per-foot correlation of height between the two views; the fit starts from an analytic IK pose and anneals a robust loss from 40 px to 6 px, under a minute per clip and 20 s on a CPU for the dragon’s roar; outputs are det.npz, overlay.mp4, motion.json, render/animation.glb and showcase.mp4.

Results per README: wolf 1.6 m, 30 bones, 36 joints, trot agreement 0.94, exam 0.94 cm mean 3D joint error; dragon 3 m, 42 bones, 50 joints with wings, take off 1.00, roar 0.93, swipe 0.85, walk 0.81; giant spider 2.4 m span, 28 bones, 40 joints, eight legs, rear up 0.99, bite 0.96, pounce 0.89; fire demon 3.6 m, 38 bones, 46 joints, wing beat 0.99, slam 0.84, roar 0.73. Every clip is H3 Max with one seed per move, which the README calls a first read, not a benchmark.

Limits stated by the authors: eight-legged walking does not fit (the views disagree about which legs are up, 0.36 to 0.49); lying down fails because training poses stay inside the joint limits; skeletons are hand-placed (UniRig is named as a possible automation); plain MiniMax H3 swapped limb colours on 2 of 5 wolf clips and 0 of 5 with the LoRA; Seedance 2.5 played the views out of step; the LoRA’s training clips are re-renders of motions solved from AI clips; the ground term knows only wolf and dragon paw names; fur and cloth need spring or tracked bones.

Requirements per README, requirements.txt and the skills: Python 3.11, torch 2.11.0 cu128, transformers 5.20.2, numpy 2.4.6, opencv-python-headless 5.0, pillow, requests; Blender 5.x on PATH or BLENDER=; an NVIDIA CUDA GPU with 24 GB to train a reader at batch 20, a few GB to read, and a CPU is enough to fit; FAL_KEY for new clips and for LoRA training, which runs on fal (about USD 12 for 1,200 steps). The example release holds four meshes, four 355 MB readers, one clip and reference per creature and a 131 MB wolf LoRA, with SHA-256 hashes in tools/examples.txt.

Aralia at the baseline animates creatures with procedural gait drivers (MultiLegDriver for quadrupeds and hexapods, hopper, flyer, float) over speciesSkeleton bone hierarchies whose bone names are the driver’s emission ids; humanoid clips play through humanoidRetarget, clipStore and skinnedClipPlayer as rotation-only in-place clips while gaits own locomotion and facing; the approved 2026-07-24 CC0 clip animation spec plans a rigged creature bestiary (path A) that bundles Mesh2Motion’s rigged creature GLBs with their own CC0 clip packs (dragon 5 clips, spider 10, snake 8) under public/creatures3d/bestiary/<species>/ behind a bestiaryByName source, excludes retargeting between creature rigs, and defers procedural creatures wearing clips; the plan-map feature is specced, not built.

Aralia already drives Blender headlessly for Rig Bench (intake, ortho renders, landmark solve, gate, contact sheet; findBlender picks the newest installed Blender without a version pin), produces textured creature masters with TRELLIS.2, and has a GCP recipe that rents a 24 GB L4 per hero job. No fal credential exists in the project’s documented credential store.
Nothing was run during this assessment; no mesh, reader, clip, LoRA or fal request entered Aralia.
inferences: AnyMove is a third path for the bestiary: author a new rigged, animated species GLB from any mesh, a TRELLIS.2 hero master included, with moves chosen by prompt, where Mesh2Motion offers fixed packs for fixed species. Its output is a self-contained rigged GLB, the unit path A consumes, so it needs none of the cross-rig retargeting the spec excludes.

Most hard dependencies already exist in Aralia’s toolchain (headless Blender, a 24 GB GPU recipe, image-to-3D masters, Entity Studio review). The genuinely new ones are a fal account with spend, Blender 5.x specifically, a Python 3.11 environment, and hand-placing joints per creature.

The stated weak spots (eight-legged walking, lying down, drift) overlap little with what a bestiary spawn needs first (idle, attack, rear, roar, wing beat), except death and lie-down, which failed on the wolf and would need another source.
Prompting moves on the spot matches Aralia’s rule that gaits own locomotion; the root path in motion.json can be dropped the way humanoidRetarget drops root translation.
Medium confidence: code, docs and skills read at a pinned commit against a known project baseline; results are the authors’ own with one seed per move; nothing was run.
unknowns: Whether Blender 5.x is installed on the Windows host and whether Rig Bench’s Blender scripts keep working beside it.
fal account availability, fal’s terms for commercial use of H3 Max output, and the real spend for one creature (mesh, two clips, GPU time).
Whether a TRELLIS.2 hero master, which can carry fused or noisy geometry, rigs cleanly with automatic weights and reads well after limb paint.
How an AnyMove GLB (its own armature, 24 fps keyframes) loads through three.js and the planned bestiary EntityHandle path, and whether clip root motion must be stripped.
Reader and fit quality on Aralia’s own creature proportions versus the four published examples.
What the credited method video and LoRA post add beyond the README.
recommendations: Keep this as research until path A of the bestiary exists or an owner chooses to pilot this path on one creature.
Pilot subject: one quadruped (a hero master or the procedural beast export used in the canid experiments), two big gestures such as rear and bite, no walking and no eight-legged subject first.
Train the reader on the existing GCP L4 recipe unless a 24 GB local GPU exists; cap fal spend and keep the repository’s fal_log.jsonl as the receipt.
Treat the GLB as a bestiary candidate under Entity Studio review; it never replaces procedural gaits, Mesh2Motion packs or accepted entities.

requiredInput: A textured creature mesh as GLB, its real size and facing, a hand-placed joint list with bone parents and joint limits (rig.json), limb paint groups and prompt words (creature.json), one action sentence per move, and a fal key for new clips.
processingSteps: Prep the mesh in Blender; build and skin the armature and paint limbs; render the two-view reference frame; generate a 5 s two-camera clip with MiniMax H3 Max on fal; render about 2,200 random poses with true joints and fine-tune the DINOv2 reader; align, split and read the clip; triangulate joints from shared heights; fit forward kinematics under joint limits to both views; apply the motion in Blender and export a GLB plus renders and a showcase video.
producedOutput: A rigged, animated GLB at 24 fps with the creature’s own armature, plus det.npz, motion.json (root path, rotation, Euler angles per bone, joints in metres), overlay and showcase videos, and quality numbers (paw agreement, reprojection error).
dependencies: Python 3.11 with torch 2.11.0 cu128, transformers 5.20.2, numpy, opencv-python-headless, pillow and requests; Blender 5.x; facebook/dinov2-with-registers-base downloaded on first use; fal endpoints for the video models and the optional LoRA trainer.
runtimeRequirements: An NVIDIA CUDA GPU with about 24 GB to train a reader (about 12 GB at batch 20) and a few GB to read; the fit runs on CPU; Blender for rendering and export; network access to fal and Hugging Face.
manualWork: Place every joint on grid views, choose framing, write one prompt per move, judge clips before capture (split screen kept, colours kept, views in step), judge fits (agreement, overlay), and add spring or tracked bones for fur or cloth.
componentTypes: A hosted learned video generator, a learned joint reader fine-tuned per creature, deterministic Blender rendering and rigging, a gradient-based forward-kinematics solver, and Agent Skills that script the stages and checks.
externalRequirements: A fal account with credit for MiniMax H3 Max (about USD 0.26 per clip) and optionally the LoRA trainer; Hugging Face downloads; a GPU host.
licenceConstraints: Code Apache-2.0; DINOv2 Apache-2.0; MiniMax H3 open weights and any LoRA on them under the MiniMax H3 community licence; hosted H3 Max output under fal’s terms, which the README says to check before shipping; Tripo meshes under Tripo’s terms; the Patch marks are not licensed.
knownLimitations: Eight-legged walking and lying-down poses do not fit; skeletons are hand-placed; video models can swap limb colours or desynchronise the views; one seed per move in the published results; the ground term is wolf- and dragon-shaped; fur and cloth need extra bones.
doesNotSolve: Mesh generation itself, automatic rigging, locomotion, blending between clips, combat timing, death and lying poses, loading the GLB into Aralia’s entity contract, or any licensing decision.

comparisons.externalApproach: Any move for any rigged creature is authored by prompting a video model and capturing the result; new moves cost about USD 0.26 and a minute each once the creature’s reader exists.
comparisons.projectApproach: Creatures move by procedural gait drivers today; the approved bestiary plan would bundle Mesh2Motion’s fixed rigged species with their fixed CC0 clip packs (dragon 5 clips, spider 10), and path B (procedural creatures wearing clips) is deferred.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: AnyMove makes the species and its move set open-ended, while Mesh2Motion fixes both; neither animates Aralia’s procedural bodies.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: A hero creature with no Mesh2Motion counterpart could still enter the bestiary with its own moves; a Mesh2Motion species with a thin pack would need an AnyMove rig of its own, since clips are not retargeted across rigs.
comparisons.evidence: README results and costs at commit 7a82a0a; docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-24-cc0-clip-animation-design.md (asset inventory, path A, out of scope) at baseline b35ea0ff; src/systems/entities3d/three/gaits/multiLegDriver.ts.
comparisons.uncertainty: No AnyMove capture of an Aralia creature exists, so quality on the project’s own meshes is unmeasured.

comparisons.externalApproach: Each creature carries its own hand-placed armature in rig.json; the exported GLB binds that armature and its clip together.
comparisons.projectApproach: speciesSkeleton names bones after driver emission ids and the pose sink throws on unknown ids; humanoid clips are retargeted onto the 17-bone biped; the bestiary plan accepts foreign rigs as self-contained GLBs behind an EntityHandle.
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: An AnyMove asset is a foreign-rig bestiary unit, not a clip for an existing Aralia skeleton.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: It fits the path-A loading contract and never the species pose sink; no bone-name mapping to speciesSkeleton should be attempted.
comparisons.evidence: blender/build_rig.py and apply_motion.py docstrings; src/systems/entities3d/three/speciesSkeleton.ts header; spec section “Rigged creature bestiary (priority 2, path A)”.

comparisons.externalApproach: Blender 5.x, Python 3.11, a 24 GB CUDA GPU for training, Hugging Face downloads and a fal account; costs on fal per clip, per mesh and per LoRA run.
comparisons.projectApproach: Rig Bench drives whatever Blender is installed with no version pin; the hero pipeline rents a 24 GB L4 on GCP per job and uses Hugging Face with a stored token; no fal credential is recorded.

experiment.question: Can AnyMove turn one Aralia quadruped mesh into a rigged GLB with two big-gesture clips whose view agreement is at least 0.8, within a fixed budget, and does that GLB load and play in three.js without touching the species pose sink?
experiment.exactInput: One quadruped mesh chosen by the owner (a hero master.glb or the procedural beast export from scripts/idea-board/experiments/export-canid-candidate-clip.mjs converted to GLB), its real length, a rig.json placed on AnyMove’s grid views, two prompts (rear up and bite, each starting and ending in the rest pose, on the spot), MiniMax H3 Max at 768P and 5 s, one seed each.
pinnedRevisions: facebook/dinov2-with-registers-base revision recorded at download time
Blender version, GPU model, driver, CUDA and torch versions recorded from the host or VM before the run
experiment.expectedOutput: runs/<creature>/clips/<move>/render/animation.glb for both moves, det.npz, motion.json, overlay and showcase videos, the dataset sample sheet, the reader’s held-out error, paw agreement per clip, fal_log.jsonl, timings and spend, and a three.js load receipt with a turntable capture, all under .agent/scratch.
experiment.projectBaseline: b35ea0ff84591e5f4f1d69c4ecc5d7bf918566fc; cloud clone inspected 2026-10-27T20:37:30Z with only Idea Board and plan-map note edits uncommitted
measurements: Reader held-out error in px per view; paw agreement and reprojection error per clip; fit time; GPU memory peak during training.
fal spend and request count; wall-clock per stage; number of clips discarded for swapped colours or broken split screen.
Three.js load: the GLB plays its clip on its own armature at 24 fps with no bone-name coupling to speciesSkeleton; rendered turntable judged against the AI clip and the showcase video.
experiment.limit: One creature, two moves, at most four generated clips, at most USD 10 on fal, at most three hours of GPU time, no LoRA training, no change to src/, public/ or the hero store, no retention of the GLB outside scratch until reviewed.
acceptanceCriteria: The reader’s held-out error is under 10 px per view and both moves reach paw agreement of at least 0.8.
The GLB loads in three.js and plays its clip on its own armature with no edits to Aralia code.
Reviewers judge both moves readable as the intended gesture on the turntable and the showcase video.
Spend and time stay inside the limits and every fal request is in fal_log.jsonl.
rejectionCriteria: Blender 5.x cannot be installed beside the host’s Rig Bench Blender, or no 24 GB GPU is available.
The reader exceeds 15 px per view, or three of four clips drift (swapped limbs or desynchronised views).
Both moves stay under 0.7 agreement, or the GLB fails to load or plays a visibly wrong pose.
Spend, time or scope exceeds the limits.
experiment.isolationBoundary: A separate AnyMove checkout and venv on the host or on a GPU VM; the mesh is a copy; the fal key lives in that checkout’s ignored .env only; outputs return as files under .agent/scratch; Aralia is read, never written.
experiment.cleanup: Delete the VM if one was used, remove the AnyMove venv, runs/ and the .env key, keep only the receipts and captures under .agent/scratch, confirm src/, public/ and the hero store unchanged, and append a dated result revision here only if the experiment is actually run.

lexicon.meaning: One image holding a front orthographic view on the left and a side orthographic view on the right at the same scale, sharing the vertical axis so a joint sits on the same pixel row in both.
A DINOv2 backbone with a heatmap head, fine-tuned on one creature’s rendered random poses, that finds every named joint in a view.
Each limb coloured differently on the mesh so the video model and the reader never swap left and right.
The rendered two-camera image of the painted creature at rest that the video model animates from.
The correlation of a foot’s height between the two views over a clip; 1 means the views show the same footfalls.
How far the fitted rig’s joints land from the read joints when projected back into each view, in pixels.
A small adapter trained on MiniMax H3 so generated clips keep the split screen, the limb colours and both views in step.
A made-up motion with known joints rendered in the same studio, read back and scored per joint in centimetres.
Aralia’s approved plan to spawn named monsters as self-contained rigged, animated GLBs beside the procedural generator.

records.title: GPU-driven open-world terrain, grass and foliage engine on WebGPU
records.summary: RedGPU 4.4.0-Alpha (redcamel/RedGPU, MIT) is a complete WebGPU-only JavaScript engine whose October 2026 alpha adds a Landscape system: tile-streamed 16-bit heightmaps, continuous LOD morphing, GPU frustum and HZB occlusion culling, multi-layer splatting with stochastic tiling, compute-baked grass and foliage drawn through render bundles and indirect draws, octahedral impostors, a scene-wide wind manager, a lake surface with character ripples, and KTX2 textures. Aralia already renders on three.js’s WebGPU path, so the engine itself is not adoptable; its value is as a readable reference for the GPU-driven techniques that answer Aralia’s CPU-bound draw cost and its canopy, ground and water gaps.
records.problem: Render a large walkable world with dense grass, forests and water on WebGPU without the CPU paying per draw, which is the exact cost that makes Aralia’s river scene slower on WebGPU than on WebGL (GG-362) and keeps forest canopy and ground detail short of the BG3 parity targets.

README.md, LICENCE.md, package.json, the src/ tree (543 TypeScript files, about 97,900 lines), the bilingual JSDoc headers of Landscape.ts, GrassManager.ts, GrassRenderer.ts, GrassCuller.ts, GrassInstanceBaker.ts, FoliageManager.ts, bakeFoliageImpostor.ts, WindManager.ts, Lake.ts, LakeInteractionManager.ts and BitmapTexture.ts, and the landscapeAndWater example were read. Nothing was built or run.
claims: Landscape.ts describes itself as the core class that integrates tile streaming, GPU-driven frustum and HZB occlusion culling, continuous LOD morphing, multi-layer splatting, and the foliage and grass ecosystems for a terrain of a given world size.

GrassManager and GrassRenderer describe large-scale grass scattering with camera-centred GPU instance baking in a compute shader, GPU frustum and distance culling, and rendering through GPURenderBundle and indirect draw calls in the main and shadow passes.

FoliageManager describes foliage type registration, sub-cell streaming, GPU culling and a depth prepass; bakeFoliageImpostor bakes base colour, world-space normal and packed ORM atlases for octahedral impostors.

Lake.ts describes a water surface mesh with real-time vertex waves and object interaction ripples; LakeInteractionManager collects meshes intersecting the surface and derives submersion strength, speed and footstep impulses.
BitmapTexture loads PNG, JPG, WebP, SVG and KTX2 compressed textures; package.json lists ktx-parse and fzstd among the build dependencies and names the version 4.4.0-Alpha under MIT.
demonstrates: A whole engine, not a library: its own renderer, materials, glTF loader, IBL and skybox, shadows, post effects, tone mapping, picking, antialiasing, camera controllers, and physics through a rapier dependency, with Korean and English JSDoc throughout.

Seven landscape examples (basicTerrain, tileStreaming, multiLayerSplatting, proceduralGrass, foliageAndImpostors, landscapeAndWater, openWorldIntegration) that import the built dist/index.js and stream a 16 x 16 grid of 512 px 16-bit PNG tiles from the author’s hosting.
implementationContains: src/landscape (core renderer, spatial tiles and GPU culler, shader library with stochastic tiling, weight-map sampler, scatter base classes, grass and foliage subsystems), src/wind/WindManager.ts, src/water/Lake.ts with lakeCore, src/utils/texture/textureParser/createGPUTextureFromKTX2.ts, and a rollup build to dist/ of about 7.8 MB; the package is not published on npm (registry lookup returned 404 on 2026-10-27).

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment from the repository at a pinned commit, the day after its alpha release; the supplied X post stayed unread. Recorded as a technique reference, not an engine candidate: Aralia is committed to three.js’s WebGPU path, and RedGPU’s GPU-driven grass, foliage, culling and splatting are the parts that speak to open Aralia gaps.

projectBaseline.dirtyNote: Cloud clone of branch ccr-2da4fbce-xouf23 at the commit named, carrying the uncommitted IB-0016 board edits; no source code differed from the baseline.

facts: RedGPU at commit 95aaf9a (2026-10-26) is an MIT-licensed, WebGPU-only JavaScript engine (package redgpu, version 4.4.0-Alpha) of 543 TypeScript files and about 97,900 lines, built with rollup to a dist/ of about 7.8 MB; it is not published on npm, and its JSDoc is written in Korean and English side by side.

Its Landscape class integrates tile streaming of a global heightmap plus 16-bit PNG height tiles chosen by a URL resolver and a loading radius, GPU-driven frustum and HZB occlusion culling of tiles, continuous LOD morphing over eight levels, multi-layer weight-map splatting with stochastic tiling in the shader library, and the foliage and grass managers; the example builds a 4,000 unit terrain with heightScale 300 and a 1,250 unit tile radius from a 16 x 16 grid of 512 px tiles.

Grass is baked onto the terrain by a compute shader in 16 m cells around the camera, culled by a compute frustum and distance pass, and drawn through GPURenderBundle plus indirect draws in the main and shadow passes, with per-type mega buffers holding near and far draw slots.

Foliage (3D meshes) is registered per type, streamed in 100 m sub-cells from a 100 m procedural seed grid, GPU-culled, drawn with a depth prepass, and baked into octahedral impostors (base colour, world normal and packed ORM atlases) for distance.

A scene-wide WindManager holds direction, speed and strength; a Lake class renders a wave surface with vertex waves, and its interaction manager turns meshes crossing the surface into submersion and footstep ripples; BitmapTexture accepts KTX2 compressed textures through ktx-parse and fzstd.

Per a web search summary of the Korean release notes (the page itself was not opened), V4.4.0-Alpha was released on 2026-10-26 and is the release that introduces these systems; a pinned post on the author’s X profile the same day announces it, and the supplied post id is in that date range but was not read.

Aralia at the baseline renders on three.js 0.172 with React Three Fiber 9, with WebGPURenderer and TSL in use across the ocean, river and probe scenes; the webgpu-migration plan-map topic has the ground probe, material parity and entity materials done, the battle-map migration active, and the default flip parked, and it names MIT TSL lifts (trees, grass, wind, clouds, sky, GI) from fable5-world-demo as the reason to build on the new renderer.

Aralia’s ground world builds chunk meshes per LOD tier from worldforge data with border skirts and a five-by-five chunk window around the player, colours terrain by biome rather than splat textures, scatters vegetation deterministically from vertex hashes on the CPU (vegetationScatter.ts) into instanced grass, understory and ez-tree fields, and uses no KTX2 textures.

GG-362 records that the river on WebGPU is CPU-bound: the same 337 to 437 draws a frame as WebGL, at about 27 µs of CPU per draw against 12 on WebGL, so whole frames run 7.5 to 21.9 ms against 7.2 to 16.6 ms; GG-341 records five water systems that never meet; the forests topic records trees reading faceted and flat-shaded up close with the canopy unjudged.
Nothing was built or run during this assessment; no file from RedGPU entered Aralia.
inferences: Adopting RedGPU is off the table: it is a second engine with its own renderer and scene graph, in alpha, not on npm, and Aralia’s migration is already half-way across three’s WebGPU path with TSL lifts planned. Two WebGPU engines cannot share one scene.

The techniques are the value. Compute-baked instances, compute culling, render bundles and indirect draws remove exactly the per-draw CPU cost that GG-362 measures, and three 0.172’s WebGPU backend exposes compute through TSL and has indirect-draw and render-bundle support whose maturity in that release is unverified.

Octahedral impostors and GPU-culled foliage sub-cells are the most direct answer to the forests topic’s faceted trees and unjudged canopy; splatting with stochastic tiling speaks to the BG3 parity ground surface; the lake’s footstep ripples speak to the ground water surface; KTX2 speaks to texture memory once the beautification catalogs grow.

Because the engine is bilingual, example-rich and MIT, it is a cheaper read than most papers for these techniques, but at about 98,000 lines it is a time sink unless the read is scoped to one subsystem at a time.
Medium confidence: module headers, the main class and one example read at a pinned commit; no render measured; the release notes and post known only through a search summary.
unknowns: Whether three 0.172’s WebGPU backend supports indirect draws and render bundles well enough for a grass port, or whether that needs a three upgrade.
Measured frame cost of RedGPU’s grass and tile streaming at a blade count and resolution comparable to Aralia’s world window.
How RedGPU’s heightmap-tile terrain source would map onto Aralia’s procedurally generated ground, which has no height tiles.
The licence of the example terrain tiles on the author’s hosting, and how stable the alpha API is between releases.
What the supplied post and the release page say beyond the indexed summaries.
recommendations: Keep this as a reference record; do not import RedGPU or run it inside Aralia.
When the GG-362 draw-cost work is picked up, read src/landscape/grass (baker, culler, renderer) first and write the TSL equivalent behind a flag in the WebGPU probe scene.
When the forests canopy is judged, read bakeFoliageImpostor.ts and the foliage sub-cell streaming as the impostor reference.
Cross-link this record from GG-362 so the next agent on that gap finds the reference without searching.

componentTypes: Deterministic GPU compute baking and culling, a hierarchical-Z occlusion pass, render bundles with indirect draws, geomorphing LOD meshes, splat materials, impostor baking, a vertex-wave water surface, and a compressed-texture loader.

comparisons.externalApproach: Instances are baked and culled in compute shaders and drawn through render bundles with indirect draws, so the CPU issues a handful of commands per frame regardless of blade or tile count.
comparisons.projectApproach: Vegetation instances are generated on the CPU per chunk and drawn as three.js instanced meshes culled per object; on three 0.172’s WebGPU path each of the river’s 337 to 437 draws costs about 27 µs of CPU against 12 on WebGL (GG-362).
comparisons.meaningfulDifference: RedGPU moves the per-draw work to the GPU; Aralia pays it on the CPU per draw, and more so on WebGPU than on WebGL.
comparisons.practicalConsequence: The technique class in RedGPU’s grass path is the remedy GG-362 needs; porting it means TSL compute for baking and culling plus indirect draws in three’s backend.
comparisons.evidence: GrassInstanceBaker.ts, GrassCuller.ts and GrassRenderer.ts headers at commit 95aaf9a; docs/projects/GLOBAL_GAPS.md GG-362; src/systems/world3d/vegetationScatter.ts at baseline b35ea0ff.
comparisons.uncertainty: Three 0.172’s indirect-draw and render-bundle support was not tested; RedGPU’s own frame cost was not measured.

lexicon.meaning: Deciding what to draw on the GPU itself, with compute shaders writing instance lists and draw arguments, so the CPU issues few commands.
A draw call whose vertex and instance counts are read from a GPU buffer, so a compute pass can fill them without a CPU round trip.
A pre-recorded sequence of WebGPU draw commands replayed each frame at almost no CPU cost.
Rejecting objects hidden behind others by testing their bounds against a hierarchical depth buffer from the previous frame.
Blending terrain vertices between two detail levels by distance so the mesh never pops when a tile changes level; also called geomorphing.
One terrain texture set blended in by a weight map channel; several layers make the ground’s surface.
Sampling a repeating texture at randomised offsets per region so the repeat pattern stops being visible.
A distant tree drawn as a card whose texture atlas holds views from many directions, picked by the viewing angle.
A container for GPU-compressed textures that stay compressed in video memory; supercompressed variants decode on load.

records.title: Consumer GeForce tensor-rate unlock for local AI compute
records.summary: GeForce cards from the 20 series on run FP16 and BF16 tensor-core matrix math with FP32 accumulation at half the rate of the professional cards built on the same chips; the halved path is the one that training, LoRA fine-tuning, diffusion models and long-prompt prefill spend their time in, while token-by-token decoding is bandwidth-bound and barely changes. Zagitta’s gpu-unlock (GPL-2.0, version 1.1.0) is a Linux kernel module that, before the NVIDIA driver binds a card, writes the speed selectors and resets the card so a GA102 to GA106 part (and, per its recipe list, an RTX 4090) issues those instructions at full rate; the author’s 3090 Ti measurements show BF16 rising from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS and TF32 nearly doubling. Aralia’s dev machine is an 8 GB RTX 2070 SUPER on Windows and its heavy AI jobs rent a data-center L4, so nothing in the project would speed up today; the record exists so the next local GPU purchase is made with this in mind.
records.problem: Aralia’s AI sidecars (creature readers, image-to-3D, mesh refinement, LoRA training) are the workloads that live on the halved tensor path, and the project rents cloud GPUs partly because the local card cannot carry them; a local consumer card that ran at professional rate would change what stays local.

sources.provenance: Shallow clone of the public repository on 2026-10-27 from a cloud session at commit 6081407b312aa3139a2bed62bdda354f4ffddc1d. README.md, VERSION, AGENTS.md and the directory layout (kernel, firmware, packaging, debian, tests, docs, licenses) were read; the kernel source was only grepped for device families. Nothing was built, installed or run, and no NVIDIA input was downloaded.
claims: The README states that the module doubles the instruction issuing speed of FP and BF16 FMA into FP32 operations on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards by writing the speed selectors (SS0 0x88888888 for the full BF16 rate and the 4-bit SS1 0x8) and performing a function-level reset before the unmodified NVIDIA driver binds the card, so no VBIOS flash or patched driver is needed.

The README’s table for a 3090 Ti dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W with FP32 accumulation lists FP16 87.46 to 118.39 TFLOPS, BF16 87.50 to 157.41 TFLOPS and TF32 42.58 to 82.61 TFLOPS, citing the repository’s issue 1.

The README’s boot section lists the supported recipes as GA100, GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106 or RTX 4090; its FAQ says Turing and Ada support exists in forks to be integrated, points Windows users at a separate impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK port, and says harm is very unlikely because standard throttling and power management stay intact.

The unlock is opt-in through the kernel command line (gpu_unlock.targets=all or PCI addresses), is applied from the initramfs before the nvidia module, clears when the card loses power, and is re-applied on resume from suspend.
demonstrates: A packaged, distribution-aware install path (Arch, Debian and Ubuntu, Fedora and RHEL) with initramfs integration and a suspend notifier, which makes the mechanism reproducible by others rather than a one-off hack.
The author’s own measurements on one card; no independent benchmark was inspected.
implementationContains: A kernel module under kernel/, firmware generation inputs and a NOTICE under firmware/, Makefile-driven packaging for three package formats, Debian packaging, tests, docs, and a licenses directory.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment from the gpu-unlock repository at a pinned commit. The project owner supplied a translated explainer of the GeForce tensor-rate throttle and this unlock in chat without naming its origin post; the explainer’s figures match the README. Recorded as a hardware-purchase and local-compute consideration, not as something to apply: Aralia’s only local GPU is an unsupported 8 GB Turing card on Windows and its rented L4 already runs at professional rate.

projectBaseline.dirtyNote: Cloud clone of branch ccr-2da4fbce-xouf23 at the commit named, carrying the uncommitted IB-0017 board edits; no source code differed from the baseline.

facts: gpu-unlock at commit 6081407 (2026-10-26) is version 1.1.0, a GPL-2.0-only Linux kernel module with Arch, Debian and RPM packaging; it combines the cmpunlocker V67/PLM technique with the pre-driver timing of an earlier UEFI approach, writes speed selectors SS0 0x88888888 and SS1 0x8, performs a function-level reset, and then lets the unmodified NVIDIA driver bind the card.

The README states the effect as doubling the instruction issue rate of FP16 and BF16 FMA into FP32 on GA102, GA103, GA104 and GA106 cards; its boot section lists GA100 and the RTX 4090 among supported recipes; the FAQ says Turing and Ada support exists in forks pending integration and names impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK as a separate Windows port.

The README’s 3090 Ti table (dense 8192³ GEMM at 450 W, FP32 accumulation, five-sample medians, citing issue 1) reads FP16 87.46 to 118.39 TFLOPS, BF16 87.50 to 157.41 TFLOPS, TF32 42.58 to 82.61 TFLOPS. The text the owner supplied quotes 87.5 to 157.4 for BF16 and “TF32 basically doubles”, which matches.

The unlock is opt-in by kernel command line, runs from the initramfs before the nvidia module, is not persistent (a card that loses power returns to the throttled state), is re-applied on resume from suspend, and skips any card a driver has already bound; the generated firmware buffer derives from a pinned CMP reference and NVIDIA firmware stays under NVIDIA’s terms per the README and firmware/NOTICE.md.

The README’s FAQ states that harm is very unlikely because the module only removes a handicap that differentiates consumer from professional cards and standard throttling and power management remain intact; it does not discuss NVIDIA’s licence terms or warranty, and web coverage from the preceding week describes long-term stability as lightly tested.

The supplied explainer, consistent with web coverage and with a public X post by KBlueleaf found by search, states that the halved path (FP16 and BF16 matrix multiply with FP32 accumulate, and FP8 on the 40 and 50 series) is where training, LoRA fine-tuning, text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion and long-prompt prefill spend their compute, that token-by-token decoding is bandwidth-bound and barely moves, that a 40-series unlock was shown on AD103 on Windows, and that the 50 series reads the selector through fuses so the same trick does not apply; the 50-series FP4 path is described as not halved. The 70 percent prefill figure for an RTX 6000 PRO against a 5090 comes only from the explainer and was not corroborated.

Aralia’s dev machine is an RTX 2070 SUPER (TU104, 8 GB, Windows host), per the river and ocean domain docs; its heavy AI jobs run on a rented GCP spot L4 (AD104, a data-center part) through tools/creatureHero/gcp; the AnyMove reader (IB-0015) needs about 12 GB and a 24 GB card, Hi3D v1.0 (IB-0014) was validated only on a 96 GB card, and TRELLIS.2 masters are made on the L4 or a hosted Space.
The game itself renders through three.js on WebGPU and WebGL and uses no tensor-core FP32-accumulate path; the throttle and the unlock concern only the AI sidecars the board assesses.
Nothing was built, installed or run during this assessment; no card was modified and no file from the repository entered Aralia.
inferences: Today the unlock changes nothing for Aralia: the local card is both unsupported by 1.1.0 (Turing) and too small (8 GB) for the sidecars, and the rented L4 is already a full-rate part.

It changes the purchase calculus: a used 3090 or 3090 Ti (24 GB, GA102) on a Linux boot would carry the AnyMove reader and TRELLIS-class jobs locally at close to A6000 matrix rate, which is the point at which the GCP L4 habit stops paying.

The Windows host is the second blocker: the kernel module is Linux-only, and WSL2 cannot load a module that touches the physical GPU because the NVIDIA driver runs on the Windows side; the separate Windows port is the only route without dual-booting, and it was not inspected.

Modifying driver-time GPU behaviour is an owner decision that touches NVIDIA’s terms and the card’s warranty, whatever the author says about physical risk; the board records the option and does not endorse it.
Medium confidence: README and layout read at a pinned commit; measurements are the author’s on one card; the supplied explainer’s origin is unknown and its one uncorroborated figure is flagged.
unknowns: Which of the five unread supplied X posts, if any, the owner’s explainer came from.
NVIDIA’s licence and warranty position on the unlock, and whether a driver update could detect or undo it.
The state of the Turing and Ada forks and of the Windows port, none of which were inspected.
Real wall-clock gains on Aralia’s actual sidecar jobs (reader training, image-to-3D, mesh refinement) rather than on a GEMM benchmark.
Whether the owner intends to buy a local 24 GB card at all.
recommendations: Record only; do not apply any unlock to the dev machine, which is unsupported and on Windows.
If a local 24 GB card is ever bought for the sidecars, prefer a GA102 part with a Linux boot and reassess this record first, including the licence and warranty question as an owner decision.
Keep the sidecar records (IB-0014, IB-0015) honest about GPU requirements in TFLOPS terms as well as VRAM, since the throttle halves throughput on consumer cards.

requiredInput: A supported NVIDIA GPU (GA100, GA102, GA103, GA104, GA106 or RTX 4090 per the README), a Linux distribution with kernel headers and an initramfs, the pinned NVIDIA driver archive fetched at build time to extract firmware, and an explicit kernel command line opt-in.
processingSteps: At boot from the initramfs, before the nvidia module binds a card: clear stray bus mastering, run the unlock firmware sequence, write the speed selectors, perform a function-level reset, then let the stock driver bind; repeat on resume from suspend.
producedOutput: A card whose FP16 and BF16 tensor instructions with FP32 accumulation issue at the professional rate until the next power loss; kernel log lines reporting each card’s result.
dependencies: Linux kernel build tooling, the NVIDIA driver archive as a build input, the packaging tools of the distribution, and the module’s generated firmware buffer.
runtimeRequirements: A Linux boot with the module in the initramfs ahead of the nvidia module; not applicable under Windows or WSL2.
manualWork: Install the package, add the kernel parameter, regenerate boot images, verify with the kernel log and lspci, and decide the licence and warranty question.
componentTypes: A kernel module, firmware sequencing derived from a reference unlocker, PCI function-level reset, initramfs hooks and a suspend notifier.
externalRequirements: Network access at build time for the NVIDIA inputs; nothing at runtime.
licenceConstraints: GPL-2.0-only for the module and packaging; the generated buffer derives from a pinned CMP reference and NVIDIA firmware remains under NVIDIA’s terms; NVIDIA’s driver licence and the card’s warranty are not addressed by the project.
knownLimitations: Linux only; Ampere plus the 4090 in 1.1.0; not persistent across power loss; lightly tested long-term stability per coverage; one OEM 3080 Ti 20 GB reportedly completed the unlock with BF16 still at half rate; the 50 series reads the selector through fuses.

lexicon.meaning: Multiplying half-precision numbers but summing the products in 32-bit floats; the mode training and diffusion use for accuracy, and the one GeForce cards run at half rate.
How many tensor-core instructions of a kind the hardware accepts per clock; the throttle halves it for the FP32-accumulate path without changing the cores.
A register the card’s firmware sets at start-up that picks the issue rate; the unlock writes the full-rate value before the driver loads.
A PCI reset of one device that restarts it without rebooting the machine; the unlock uses it after writing the selectors.
The step where a language model reads the whole prompt at once; compute-bound and on the halved path, unlike the bandwidth-bound decode of one token at a time.
The full tensor throughput of RTX A-series, RTX PRO and data-center cards built on the same chips as the consumer parts.

records.title: Full-duplex speech-to-speech NPC personas from a text role prompt
records.summary: PersonaPlex (NVIDIA, code MIT, weights under the NVIDIA Open Model License) is a 7B real-time speech-to-speech model built on Kyutai’s Moshi that listens and talks at the same time, so it pauses, interrupts and backchannels like a person, and takes its persona from a text role prompt plus one of 18 packaged voices. It ships a Python WebSocket server, a React web client with an Opus decoder, and an offline evaluator. Aralia voices NPCs today by chaining a text model (Ollama or Groq) with Gemini text-to-speech and playing 24 kHz PCM, the rate PersonaPlex speaks at; its NPC knowledge profiles already have the shape of the model’s customer-service “Information:” prompts. The model needs a CUDA GPU with room for 7B bfloat16 weights, is English-trained, and would be a presentation layer: game effects would still come from the transcript through the intent reader.
records.problem: Let a player talk to an Aralia NPC with their voice and hear it answer in character without the turn-by-turn lag of recognise, think, then synthesise, while the game’s dialogue state, skill checks and combat triggers keep working from what was said.

README.md, LICENSE-MIT, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yaml, moshi/pyproject.toml, the argument lists of moshi/server.py and moshi/offline.py, the loader’s dtype and repository constants, the client’s package.json, README, protocol types and the Conversation page’s URL construction were read. Nothing was installed or run, no weights were downloaded, and the model licence was not accepted.
claims: The README describes a real-time, full-duplex speech-to-speech conversational model with persona control through text role prompts and audio voice conditioning, based on the Moshi architecture and weights, trained on synthetic conversations (a fixed assistant role and varied customer-service roles) and on real conversations from the Fisher English Corpus with LLM-labelled prompts.

The server is started with python -m moshi.server --ssl, serves a web UI on port 8998, and accepts --cpu-offload (with the accelerate package) when GPU memory is insufficient; Blackwell GPUs need a CUDA 13 torch install per the README.

Eighteen packaged voices are listed (NATF0 to NATF3, NATM0 to NATM3, VARF0 to VARF4, VARM0 to VARM4); the client appends text_prompt and voice_prompt as query parameters on the /api/chat WebSocket URL, and the server resolves the voice to a file in its voice-prompt directory.

The README’s prompting guide shows customer-service roles that carry facts after an “Information:” marker, casual roles that start “You enjoy having a good conversation.”, and an astronaut prompt offered as an out-of-distribution example the model handles plausibly.

The loader defaults to bfloat16 and reads model.safetensors plus a Mimi tokenizer checkpoint from nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1; pyproject pins torch at 2.2 to below 2.5 and needs the Opus development library.
demonstrates: A complete serving stack rather than a checkpoint: a Dockerfile on the CUDA 12.4.1 runtime image with GPU reservation, a React 18 and Vite client with an Opus WebAssembly decoder and a typed WebSocket protocol (handshake, audio, text, control, metadata, error, ping), and an offline script that turns an input wav and a role prompt into an output wav and a text JSON.
The authors’ own description of turn-taking quality; no latency figure is given in the README and none was measured here.
implementationContains: moshi/ (server, offline evaluator, models including the LM with text and voice prompt handling, loaders), client/ (the Kyutai-derived web client under MIT), assets/test (two input wavs and a service prompt), Dockerfile and compose file.

revisions.changeSummary: Initial assessment from the repository at a pinned commit, the day the owner supplied it. The serving stack is complete and the persona mechanism maps cleanly onto Aralia’s NPC knowledge profiles and speech profiles, and the game already plays 24 kHz PCM for NPC speech, so a bounded sidecar trial is cheap to define. The model’s GPU footprint, English-only training, and the fact that it is a presentation layer rather than a game-logic model are the limits.

projectBaseline.dirtyNote: Cloud clone of branch ccr-2da4fbce-xouf23 at the commit named, carrying the uncommitted IB-0018 board edits; no source code differed from the baseline.

facts: PersonaPlex at commit 3428dfd (2026-03-02) is MIT-licensed code around a 7B speech-to-speech model whose weights sit on Hugging Face under the NVIDIA Open Model License behind a licence gate; the paper is arXiv 2602.06053 (February 2026) from NVIDIA ADLR.

The model is full duplex: it updates its state as the user speaks and streams audio and text back at once, so it can pause, interrupt and backchannel; persona comes from a text role prompt and a voice embedding chosen from 18 packaged voices, passed per session as text_prompt and voice_prompt query parameters on the /api/chat WebSocket.

Training covered a fixed assistant role, varied customer-service roles whose prompts carry facts after an “Information:” marker, and real English conversations from the Fisher corpus; the README encourages out-of-distribution prompts and ships an astronaut-in-a-reactor-meltdown example as proof the Helium backbone generalises.

Serving needs a CUDA GPU (the loader defaults to bfloat16, so the 7B weights alone are on the order of 14 GB before activations; the README gives no figure and offers --cpu-offload), Python 3.10 or newer, torch 2.2 to below 2.5, the Opus development library, and an HF_TOKEN; a Dockerfile on the CUDA 12.4.1 runtime image and a compose file with a GPU reservation are included, and Blackwell GPUs need a CUDA 13 torch build.

The React 18 and Vite client (MIT, derived from Kyutai’s moshi-client) captures microphone audio, sends and receives Opus over the WebSocket with a WebAssembly decoder worker, shows the streamed text, and exposes sampling parameters; an offline script evaluates a wav file against a role prompt and writes the agent’s audio and text.

Aralia at the baseline voices NPCs by chaining a text model with Gemini text-to-speech: ttsService.synthesizeSpeech (default voice Kore) is called from handleNpcInteraction and handleOracle, and useAudio.playPcmAudio plays 24 kHz, 16-bit, mono PCM through a Web Audio context; the chain needs a Gemini API key.

Aralia’s NPC text pipeline is Ollama locally or Groq through textProviderRouter with no fallback; geminiService and the Ollama banter service prompt the model to answer in the NPC’s voice in one or two sentences; each NPC carries a SpeechProfile (a per-NPC text voice signature with culture lexicons), a personality archetype from role and biome, quirks, and a knowledge profile that the dialogue topic (DIAL) work already feeds into the AI dialogue prompt.

Aralia’s game logic reads conversation text: the universal intent reader classifies every line as talk, skill, flee, attack or ambiguous and can turn a peaceful scene violent; topic-based dialogue graphs carry prerequisites, costs, skill checks and unlocks; the conversation panel gates player turns and pending responses; the ai-arbiter topic’s “NPC embodiment (think as the NPC)” feature is specced, not built.

The dev machine is an RTX 2070 SUPER with 8 GB, which cannot hold 7B bfloat16 weights; the project already rents a 24 GB GCP L4 per hero job and runs a local Ollama; the game is a browser application served by Vite.
Nothing was installed or run during this assessment; no weights, licence acceptance, audio or token entered Aralia.
inferences: PersonaPlex would replace the recognise-think-synthesise chain for live conversation with one model, and the persona prompt can be composed from what Aralia already has: the archetype and speech profile for manner, the knowledge profile as the “Information:” block, and a packaged voice chosen per NPC.

It is a presentation layer, not a game-logic model: its streamed text is a transcript of what the NPC said, so skill checks, unlocks and combat triggers would still come from feeding that transcript (and the player’s) through the intent reader and dialogue state, and scripted topic graphs would have to be expressed as prompt facts rather than enforced.

The serving footprint rules out the dev machine’s GPU and any player machine; a trial runs the server on the rented L4 or a similar card and the browser talks to it, which the shipped client already shows is a WebSocket plus Opus problem Aralia’s React app can absorb.
English-only training and customer-service-shaped roles are the quality risk for fantasy NPCs; the README’s own out-of-distribution example is the reason to test rather than assume.
Medium confidence: code, README and client read at a pinned commit; no audio was heard; the model licence and paper were not read.
unknowns: The terms of the NVIDIA Open Model License for a shipped game and for hosting the model for players.
Actual GPU memory and end-to-end latency on a 24 GB card, and whether --cpu-offload is usable at conversational latency.
How well a fantasy NPC role prompt holds persona and facts over a ten-minute conversation, and how the model handles player lines that the intent reader would class as skill or attack.
Whether the Opus WebSocket transport and microphone capture fit inside Aralia’s conversation panel without a separate page.
Languages beyond English, and the 18 voices’ fit to Aralia’s cultures and species.
recommendations: Treat as a sidecar trial, not a replacement for the text dialogue pipeline, which keeps owning game effects.

Compose one NPC’s role prompt from the archetype, speech profile and knowledge profile the game already produces, pick one natural voice, and talk to it through the stock client on a rented 24 GB GPU before touching any Aralia code.
Record the transcript stream and run it through resolvePlayerIntent offline to see whether the existing reader could govern a spoken scene.
Read the model licence before any demo leaves the dev machine.

requiredInput: A text role prompt, a voice embedding name from the packaged set, live microphone audio from the player over a WebSocket, and sampling parameters; for offline evaluation, a wav file and a prompt.
processingSteps: The Mimi codec tokenises incoming audio; the Moshi-derived language model (Helium backbone) conditions on the role prompt tokens and the voice prompt embedding and streams joint audio and text tokens while listening; the server encodes the audio as Opus frames and sends text alongside; the client decodes and plays while still sending the user’s audio.
producedOutput: A continuous spoken response with backchannels and interruptions, plus the streamed text of what the agent says; offline, an output wav of the same length as the input and a JSON transcript.
dependencies: The moshi-personaplex package (torch, aiohttp, sphn, sentencepiece, sounddevice, safetensors, huggingface-hub, einops), the Opus development library, the gated weights, and for the client Node, React 18, Vite and the Opus decoder worker.
runtimeRequirements: A CUDA GPU able to hold the 7B bfloat16 model plus the Mimi codec, or CPU offload at some latency cost; a server process on port 8998 with TLS for microphone access; a browser with microphone permission.
manualWork: Accept the model licence, obtain a token, write and tune role prompts, choose voices, host the server, and judge conversations by ear.
componentTypes: A learned speech-to-speech transformer, a neural audio codec, a WebSocket streaming server, an Opus-based browser client, and an offline evaluation harness.
externalRequirements: Hugging Face access for the weights, a GPU host, and acceptance of the NVIDIA Open Model License.
licenceConstraints: Code MIT; upstream Moshi and AudioCraft licences retained under moshi/; weights under the NVIDIA Open Model License, unread, which must be reviewed for hosting and distribution before any use beyond a private trial.
knownLimitations: English-trained; roles trained as assistant and customer service with facts; 7B weights need a sizeable GPU; no stated latency; persona drift and fact hallucination over long conversations are unmeasured; no game-state awareness.
doesNotSolve: Dialogue state, skill checks, quest unlocks, combat triggers, NPC memory, non-English speech, player-side hardware, or the licence question.

experiment.question: Can one Aralia NPC, with a role prompt composed from its archetype, speech profile and knowledge profile, hold a ten-minute spoken conversation in character on PersonaPlex with latency and interruption that feel natural, and does its transcript let the existing intent reader classify the player’s lines sensibly?
experiment.exactInput: One existing NPC chosen by the dialogue owner, a role prompt written by hand from that NPC’s archetype, speech profile and knowledge profile in the customer-service “Information:” shape, one natural voice (NATM or NATF), the stock server and client on a rented 24 GB GPU, seed fixed, default sampling, and a scripted list of twelve player lines covering talk, a skill attempt, an insult and an attack.
pinnedRevisions: nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1 weights revision recorded at download time
GPU model, driver, CUDA and torch versions recorded from the host before the run
experiment.expectedOutput: A recording of the conversation, the streamed transcript, measured first-audio latency per turn, a count of persona breaks and fact errors against the prompt, the intent reader’s classification of each scripted player line run offline from the transcript, and a short verdict, all under .agent/scratch.
experiment.projectBaseline: b35ea0ff84591e5f4f1d69c4ecc5d7bf918566fc; cloud clone inspected 2026-10-27T22:04:12Z with only Idea Board edits uncommitted
measurements: First-audio latency per turn and the number of successful interruptions.
Persona breaks, fact errors and out-of-world references in ten minutes.
Intent reader agreement with the scripted intent of each player line.
GPU memory and server wall-clock.
experiment.limit: One NPC, one voice, one session of at most ten minutes, at most two hours of rented GPU, the stock client only, no Aralia code change, no player audio beyond the owner’s own.
acceptanceCriteria: The model stays in the NPC’s role and uses the knowledge-profile facts correctly for most of the session, with no more than two fact errors.
Interruptions and backchannels work and first-audio latency feels conversational to the owner.
The intent reader classifies at least ten of the twelve scripted lines as intended from the transcript.
rejectionCriteria: The model drops the fantasy role or answers as a generic assistant repeatedly.
Latency or memory makes the session unusable on a 24 GB card.
The licence forbids the intended use, or the intent reader misreads most spoken lines.
experiment.isolationBoundary: A rented GPU host running the stock PersonaPlex server and client; the role prompt is a scratch file; Aralia is read only for the NPC data and the offline intent-reader run.
experiment.cleanup: Delete the host and its weights cache, keep the recording, transcript and measurements under .agent/scratch, and append a dated result revision here only if the experiment is actually run.

lexicon.meaning: Listening and speaking at the same time in one model, so it can pause, interrupt and acknowledge while the other person talks.
A short acknowledgement such as “uh-huh” given while the other person is still speaking.
The text that sets the agent’s identity, manner and facts for a session; PersonaPlex’s customer-service prompts carry facts after “Information:”.
Choosing the agent’s voice by a packaged audio embedding rather than by text.
The neural audio codec that turns speech into tokens the language model consumes and produces, at 24 kHz.
Aralia’s per-NPC set of facts injected into the AI dialogue prompt; the natural source of a role prompt’s facts.
Aralia’s classifier that reads every conversation line as talk, skill, flee, attack or ambiguous and triggers game effects.
